   427|## Chapter 9 — Why AI Projects Fail in Six Weeks
   428|
   429|I've watched eight different businesses try to adopt AI agents. Three succeeded. Five failed. The failures all followed the same pattern. Week one: excitement. Week two: setup. Week three: demos. Week four: complications. Week five: frustration. Week six: abandonment.
   430|
   431|The six-week death spiral is real. I've lived it myself. Our first attempt at an agent system at MIFECO died in exactly six weeks. We spent three weeks building something overly complex, two weeks trying to make it work, and one week admitting it wasn't working and quietly shutting it down. The pattern is so predictable that I can now spot it before it happens.
   432|
   433|Three things kill AI projects in the first six weeks. If you can avoid these three traps, you have a real shot at building something that lasts.
   434|
   435|**Trap one: scope creep.**
   436|
   437|The team starts with a clear goal. "We'll build a lead response agent." That's specific. That's manageable. But by the end of week two, someone has suggested adding features. "Can it also qualify leads?" Sure. "Can it update the CRM?" Easy. "Can it generate proposals?" That's more work, but fine. "Can it handle objections in live chat?" Now we're building a completely different system.
   438|
   439|This is how a two-week project becomes a six-week project that never finishes. Every feature addition multiplies the complexity. The lead response agent we started building needed to read email, generate text, and send it. Simple. The lead response plus qualification plus CRM update plus proposal generation plus live chat agent needed to integrate with three APIs, maintain state across multiple workflows, handle a dozen edge cases, and never make a mistake. That's a six-month engineering project, not a six-week pilot.
   440|
   441|The fix is brutal simplicity. Define exactly one thing the agent will do. Nothing else. Write it down. "This agent sends an initial response to every inbound lead within two minutes." That's the spec. Everything else is out of scope. If the agent does that one thing reliably, you've won. You can add features later. Schedule them for month two. Don't add them in week two. I've seen too many teams build a Swiss Army knife and end up with a tool that opens nothing well.
   442|
   443|**Trap two: tool addiction.**
   444|
   445|AI builders love tools. New models come out every week. New frameworks. New platforms. New vector databases. Each one promises to solve a problem you don't have yet. The team starts with a simple architecture. By week three, they're debating whether to switch from LangChain to CrewAI, whether to use GPT-4o or Claude 3.5, whether to store embeddings in Pinecone or Weaviate. None of these decisions matter for a simple agent. They're distractions.
   446|
   447|I fell into this hard on our first attempt. We spent a week evaluating different language models, comparing latency benchmarks, reading blog posts about which framework was best. We never wrote a line of application code. We built a demo using three different frameworks and then couldn't figure out which one was causing the bugs.
   448|
   449|The fix is to pick the simplest possible stack and start building. Use the model you already have access to. Don't add a vector database until you have a use case that requires one. Don't switch frameworks because of a blog post. The first version of any agent should use the least number of technologies that could possibly work. You can optimize later.
   450|
   451|**Trap three: feedback loop abandonment.**
   452|
   453|This is the deadliest trap. The team builds the agent. They test it with sample inputs. It works. They deploy it to production. And then they stop looking at it.
   454|
   455|An agent in production is never finished. It encounters inputs you didn't anticipate. It makes mistakes you didn't plan for. It encounters edge cases that break your assumptions. If you don't watch it, review its outputs, and fix its failures, it will gradually degrade until it's producing garbage. And everyone will conclude the agent doesn't work.
   456|
   457|Our first MIFECO agent worked beautifully for the first three days. Then a lead emailed in Spanish. The agent responded in English, never asked for clarification, and assigned a wrong priority score. Another lead asked a question the agent wasn't designed to answer. The agent hallucinated a response and promised a feature we didn't have. Another lead had an email typo that bounced. The agent retried five times and then marked the lead as uninterested.
   458|
   459|We weren't watching. We were busy building the next feature. By the time we checked the logs, seven leads had received bad responses, one had complained to our support team, and our salesperson had to do damage control. We blamed the model. It wasn't the model's fault. It was our fault for not monitoring.
   460|
   461|The fix is a daily review ritual. Every morning, look at the agent's outputs from the previous day. Read the emails it sent. Check the decisions it made. Identify the mistakes. Fix them. Update the instructions. Add guardrails. The first month of any agent deployment requires daily attention. You're training the agent by correcting its mistakes, the same way you'd train a new employee. If you abandon the feedback loop, the agent stagnates.
   462|
   463|The businesses that succeed with agents treat deployment as the start of the process, not the end. They schedule monitoring time. They review logs. They iterate on prompts and rules based on actual production data. They accept that the first version will have flaws and they commit to fixing them.
   464|
   465|The businesses that fail treat deployment as the finish line. They build, launch, and move on to the next shiny thing.    466|
   467|The six-week death spiral is avoidable. Keep the scope to one thing. Use the simplest stack you can. Watch the outputs every day. If you do those three things, you'll still be running your agent six months from now. Most businesses won't. That's your advantage.

   660|
   661|An agent without tools is a parrot. It can repeat information. It cannot change anything. The power of an agent comes from what it can reach: your email system, your calendar, your CRM, your database, your shipping platform, your payment processor.
   662|
   663|But connecting an agent to your tools is where most implementations break. The agent gets too much access and causes damage. Or it gets too little and cannot do anything useful. Finding the balance is the hardest engineering decision you will make.

   665|I will walk through the three integration methods I use at MIFECO, the permission model that keeps us out of trouble, and the distinction between talking and acting that every agent builder needs to understand.
   666|
   667|Method one is webhooks. This is the simplest integration. Your agent constructs an HTTP request to a webhook URL, and the receiving system processes it. Webhooks work for sending data outward.    668|
   669|We use webhooks for actions that are fire-and-forget. When the lead responder processes a lead, it fires a webhook to our Slack channel with the lead summary. The webhook takes a JSON payload, Slack renders it, done. No response expected. No error handling needed beyond a retry.
   670|
   671|Method two is APIs. This is the standard approach. Your agent calls an authenticated REST endpoint, sends parameters, gets a response. APIs work for both reading and writing. They also introduce complexity: authentication, rate limits, error handling, pagination.
   672|
   673|Our logistics coordinator agent calls the shipping API about two hundred times per day. It checks shipment status, updates delivery windows, and flags exceptions.    678|

   699|The distinction between talking and acting is the framework that guides all of this.

   705|My rule: default to talking, escalate to acting only when the cost of inaction exceeds the cost of a mistake.
   706|
   707|The lead responder talks. it drafts emails. It does not act—it does not send them. The logistics coordinator talks—it suggests delivery window changes. It acts on one thing—logging tracking events, which is low-risk and high-frequency.
   708|
   709|Your agents should follow the same pattern. Give them plenty of talking tools. Give them acting tools sparingly, with approval gates, and with hard permission enforcement at the integration layer, not the agent layer. The agent can suggest anything it wants. The tool system only executes what is allowed.
   710|
   711|## Chapter 15 — Human-in-the-Loop
   712|
   713|The question I get most often from other founders is not about technology. It is about trust. "How do I know the agent will not screw something up?" The answer is that you do not know. So you design for that uncertainty.
   714|
   715|I use three modes for agent operation. Full auto, where the agent acts without approval. Approve-first, where the agent proposes and a human authorizes. Review-after, where the agent acts immediately and a human inspects the result later. Each mode serves a different function. Picking the wrong mode for a given function is where the real failures happen.
   716|
   717|Full auto is for actions where speed matters more than perfection, and the cost of a mistake is low. At MIFECO, our monitoring agent runs in full auto. It checks system health metrics every five minutes. If it detects an anomaly. CPU spike, error rate jump, queue backlog—it creates a diagnostic report and posts it to our incident channel. It does not ask permission. It just does it. The cost of a false alarm is a few seconds of reading time. The cost of a missed alarm is a production outage. Full auto is the right call.
   718|
   719|Another full auto example is our logging agent. Every agent run is logged with a structured record: prompt, tool calls, decisions, outcome. The logging agent writes these to the database automatically. If it wrote a bad record, I would notice in the weekly review. If it failed to write a record, I would have no audit trail. Full auto ensures the audit trail exists.
   720|
   721|Approve-first is for actions where accuracy matters and a human can add value by reviewing before execution. This is where most of our agents operate. The lead responder drafts emails but does not send them until Jenny approves. The contract reviewer flags unusual clauses but does not suggest redlines until legal reviews. The escalation handler proposes a resolution path but does not execute it until the shift lead confirms.
   722|
   723|Approve-first adds latency. The lead responder's email sits in a queue for an average of forty minutes before someone reviews it. That is forty minutes slower than a fully automated system. But it is also forty minutes of protection against the kind of mistake that costs a customer relationship.
   724|
   725|I learned this the hard way. Early on, I ran the lead responder in full auto mode for a week. It sent one hundred and thirty-seven emails. One of them contained a pricing hallucination. The agent quoted a price thirty percent below our actual rate. The lead replied and wanted to buy at that price. We had to honor it because the email was sent from our domain. That mistake cost us about twelve hundred dollars in margin. Approve-first would have caught it because Jenny would have seen the price and corrected it before send.
   726|
   727|Review-after is for actions where execution speed is critical and the review can happen asynchronously. Our logistics coordinator runs in review-after mode. When a shipment is delayed, the agent updates the delivery window in the customer portal immediately. Then it flags the update for review. The logistics team checks the flagged updates at the end of each shift. By then, most customers have already seen the updated window and adjusted their plans. If the update was wrong, the team corrects it and the customer gets a notification. The cost of a wrong update is a correction. The benefit of an immediate update is customer trust.
   728|
   729|The framework I use to decide which mode to use has three variables.
   730|
   731|First variable: reversibility. Can the action be undone? Sending an email is irreversible. Updating a lead score is reversible. Creating a support ticket is reversible. Deleting a record is not. Irreversible actions default to approve-first. Reversible actions can go up to review-after or full auto depending on the other variables.
   732|
   733|Second variable: velocity. How fast does the action need to happen? A shipment delay notification needs to happen within minutes. A contract review can take hours. A lead response can take tens of minutes. Higher velocity pushes toward full auto or review-after. Lower velocity pushes toward approve-first.
   734|
   735|Third variable: confidence. How sure are we that the agent will make the right call? Confidence comes from testing. If the agent has processed a thousand similar cases with a ninety-five percent accuracy rate, confidence is high. If the agent is new or the use case is novel, confidence is low. Low confidence means approve-first. High confidence means consider full auto or review-after.
   736|
   737|The three variables form a decision matrix. High irreversibility plus low confidence equals approve-first. Low irreversibility plus high velocity plus moderate confidence equals review-after. Low irreversibility plus high confidence equals full auto.
   738|
   739|Here is how this plays out for a function we added recently. The reporting agent sends weekly performance summaries to department heads. The action is sending an email with a PDF attachment. Irreversibility is low. the email can be recalled or followed up with a correction. Velocity is low—weekly reports are not urgent. Confidence is high after three months of testing. So we run it in full auto. The agent generates the report, attaches the PDF, and sends it. No review. No approval. It has been running for six weeks without a mistake.
   740|
   741|Compare that to the customer-facing price quote agent. Same action. sending an email with a document. But irreversibility is high—a wrong price quote is legally binding in many cases. Velocity is moderate—customers expect a quote within hours, not days. Confidence is moderate after testing. So we run it in review-after, but with a twist. The agent sends the quote to the customer and CCs the sales rep. The rep sees the quote immediately and can follow up if anything is wrong. The quote goes out fast, but the rep has eyes on it within seconds.
   742|
   743|The mistake most companies make is choosing one mode for everything. They either lock everything down with approve-first, killing speed, or they let everything run on full auto, creating risk. The right approach is per-function mode selection, reviewed and adjusted monthly.
   744|
   745|I keep a spreadsheet. One row per agent. Columns for function, mode, justification, and incident count. If an agent has zero incidents in its current mode for three months, I consider moving it to a less restrictive mode. If an agent has incidents, I move it to a more restrictive mode.
   746|
   747|The goal is not to eliminate human involvement. The goal is to put human involvement exactly where it adds value and remove it where it adds delay.

   749|## Chapter 16 — Memory: Why Agents Forget
   750|
   751|I had a conversation with our logistics coordinator agent that made me want to throw my laptop out the window.
   752|
   753|"Check shipment 44982," I said.
   754|
   755|The agent checked. "Shipment 44982 is delayed. The new estimated delivery is Tuesday."
   756|
   757|"What was the original delivery date?"
   758|
   759|The agent paused. Then it called the shipment API again, looking for the original date. It found it. "Monday."
   760|
   761|"Check shipment 44983," I said.
   762|
   763|The agent checked. "Shipment 44983 is on time."
   764|
   765|"And what about the delayed one? 44982?"
   766|
   767|The agent did not know what I was talking about. It had already forgotten about 44982. It asked me to clarify which shipment I meant. I had just told it. Twenty seconds earlier.
   768|
   769|This is the fundamental problem with agent memory. The agents do not remember anything beyond their immediate context window unless you explicitly build memory into the system. The language model has no persistent state. Every interaction starts fresh.
   770|
   771|There are two kinds of memory you need to understand. Short-term memory is the conversation window. The current session. What the agent just did. Long-term memory is persistent storage. Information the agent can access across sessions.
   772|
   773|Short-term memory is handled by the context window. Every time the agent makes a decision, generates a response, or calls a tool, the history of that interaction gets appended to the next request. The model sees everything that happened so far in this session.
   774|
   775|The limit is the context window size. Most models support between 8,000 and 128,000 tokens. A token is roughly three-quarters of a word. So 128,000 tokens is about 96,000 words. That sounds like a lot. It is not.
   776|
   777|Every tool call eats tokens. The tool description. The parameters. The return value. A single CRM lookup can consume 500 tokens. A company enrichment call consumes 1,000. An email draft consumes 1,500. After ten interactions, you have used 30,000 tokens just on tool overhead. The actual conversation is a fraction of that.
   778|
   779|At MIFECO, we handle the short-term memory problem with a sliding window. We keep the last three interactions plus a summary of everything before that. The summary is generated by the agent itself. After every fifth interaction, the agent produces a one-paragraph summary of the conversation so far. That summary replaces the older history in the next context window.
   780|
   781|This approach keeps our costs predictable. Each agent run costs between 2,000 and 5,000 tokens, depending on complexity. Without the sliding window, a long-running agent session could hit 50,000 tokens. At that point, the cost of the conversation exceeds the value of the work being done.
   782|
   783|Long-term memory is a different problem. The agent needs to remember facts across sessions. Customer preferences. Previous orders. Past interactions. This is not something the language model handles naturally. You have to build it.
   784|
   785|I tried several approaches before finding one that works. The first was storing everything in a vector database. Every interaction was embedded and stored. When a new interaction started, the agent searched for relevant past interactions and injected them into the context. This is the standard RAG approach. It worked poorly for us. The agent pulled up irrelevant memories, missed relevant ones, and spent more tokens reading old conversations than handling new ones.
   786|
   787|The second approach was structured memory. Instead of storing raw conversations, we store structured facts. Customer X prefers email over phone. Customer Y has a net-60 payment term. Customer Z always complains about shipping speed. These are key-value pairs stored in a simple database. The agent queries them by customer ID when a session starts.
   788|
   789|This works better. The agent gets exactly the information it needs, no more. The token cost is minimal because the facts are short and targeted. The downside is maintenance. Someone has to write the facts. Our agents can suggest facts to add to memory, but a human reviews and approves them before they go in.
   790|
   791|The third approach, which is what we use now, is a hybrid. Short-term memory uses the sliding window with summaries. Long-term memory uses structured facts with human approval. But we also have a third layer: operational memory.
   792|
   793|Operational memory is the state of the agent's work. What tasks are in progress. What tools have been called. What decisions have been made. This is stored in a JSON object that persists for the duration of a workflow. When the lead responder processes a lead, the operational memory tracks the current step. Step one: CRM check complete. Step two: enrichment in progress. Step three: scoring pending. If the agent gets interrupted, it picks up from the last completed step.
   794|
   795|This matters more than you might think. Agents fail. API calls time out. Model responses are malformed. The user closes the browser. Operational memory means the agent does not start over. It resumes.
   796|
   797|The cost trade-off is straightforward.
   798|
   799|More memory means more tokens per call. Tokens cost money. At our volume, each additional 1,000 tokens of memory costs about three cents. Over twenty thousand runs per month, that is six hundred dollars for a modest increase in memory depth.
   800|
   801|Less memory means the agent forgets things and makes mistakes. Each mistake costs time. Jenny spends twenty minutes fixing an agent error. At her hourly rate, that is about ten dollars per mistake. If the agent makes five mistakes per week due to memory failures, that is two hundred dollars per week.
   802|
   803|The math says invest in memory until the token cost exceeds the mistake cost. For us, that point is around four thousand tokens of context per agent run. That includes the sliding window history, the structured facts, and the operational memory.
   804|
   805|Here is what I recommend for someone starting out. Do not build a vector database on day one. Start with no memory beyond the raw conversation window. See where the agent fails. Add a summary window when conversations exceed ten turns. Add structured facts when the agent starts repeating itself across sessions. Add operational memory when the agent cannot handle interruptions.
   806|
   807|Each layer solves a specific failure mode. Adding all three at once is overengineering. Adding none of them means your agent will forget what it did twenty seconds ago, and you will want to throw your laptop out the window.
   808|
   809|## Chapter 17 — Prompt Design (Not Engineering)
   810|
   811|I hate the term prompt engineering. It implies that writing good prompts is a technical skill on par with writing good code. It is not. Prompting is writing. It is clear communication with an AI system. You do not need to be an engineer to be good at it. You need to be precise.
   812|
   813|The difference between a prompt that works once and a prompt that works reliably is structure. A one-shot prompt is something you write for a specific situation. You are asking the model a question, you get an answer, you move on. A reliable prompt is something you write for production. It runs hundreds or thousands of times. It handles edge cases. It produces consistent output.
   814|
   815|At MIFECO, every production prompt follows the same template. Role, rules, examples. Three sections. No deviations.
   816|
   817|The role section defines who the agent is and what it is supposed to do. I wrote earlier about the lead responder's role. Let me show you the exact text.
   818|
   819|"You are a lead qualification and outreach assistant for MIFECO, a logistics technology company. You work for the sales team. Your job is to process incoming leads from the website contact form. You research the lead and their company, score the lead on a scale of 1 to 5, and draft a personalized initial email. You do not send the email. You submit it for human review. You never make up information about a lead or company. If you cannot find reliable information, you note the gap and proceed with what you have."
   820|
   821|That is the role section. It establishes identity, function, boundaries, and failure mode. It tells the agent what to do, what not to do, and what to do when things go wrong.
   822|
   823|The role section is not a personality. It is a job description. I do not tell the agent to be friendly, helpful, or professional. Those are vague, and the agent interprets them differently every time. I tell the agent exactly what steps to follow and exactly what constraints to respect.
   824|
   825|The rules section lists constraints. Every rule is a specific behavior, not a general principle.
   826|
   827|Rule one: always check CRM for existing records before doing any research. Rule two: if the CRM check returns a record with contact date within thirty days, mark as duplicate and skip. Rule three: use the company enrichment tool before scoring. Rule four: the score field must be an integer between 1 and 5. Rule five: the email draft must include the lead's specific question or comment in the first paragraph. Rule six: if any tool returns an error, note the error in the output and continue with available data.
   828|
   829|Each rule exists because an earlier version of the agent violated it. Rule one exists because the agent once enriched a company that was already in CRM, wasting a tool call and returning redundant data. Rule three exists because the agent once scored a lead before looking up the company, giving a high score to someone with no discernible company. Rule six exists because the agent once failed silently when the enrichment tool timed out, producing an empty profile without flagging the issue.
   830|
   831|The rules are a record of failures. Every time the agent makes a mistake, I add a rule to prevent it from happening again. The rules section grows over time. It started with two rules. It now has fourteen across all agents. Not every rule applies to every agent.
   832|
   833|The examples section is the most powerful part of the prompt. I include three to five complete examples of the agent doing its job. Each example shows the input, the thought process, the tool calls, and the final output. The examples are real. They come from actual agent runs that were approved by a human.
   834|
   835|Here is a condensed example from the lead responder prompt.
   836|
   837|Input: John Smith, Acme Logistics, john@acme.com, "We need help with international shipping tracking."
   838|
   839|Thought: This is a logistics company. They have a specific need. Medium score potential. Check CRM first.
   840|
   841|Tool call: CRM search for Acme Logistics. Result: no existing record.
   842|
   843|Tool call: Company enrichment for Acme Logistics. Result: 200 employees, logistics sector, founded 2018, estimated revenue 50M.
   844|
   845|Lead score: 4 out of 5. Medium-high priority. Established company, clear need, relevant industry.
   846|
   847|Draft: "Hi John, thanks for reaching out. You mentioned international shipping tracking. MIFECO's logistics platform supports real-time tracking across 40 carriers globally. Would you be available for a brief call this week to discuss your requirements?"
   848|
   849|Output: Score 4, draft attached, no duplicates found.
   850|
   851|That example took me five minutes to write. It has saved me hours of debugging. The agent now produces outputs that look exactly like that example ninety-three percent of the time.
   852|
   853|The template works because it replaces ambiguity with structure. Without the role section, the agent does not know its boundaries. Without the rules section, the agent makes the same mistakes repeatedly. Without the examples, the agent invents its own output format and it changes every time.
   854|
   855|The difference between a works-once prompt and a works-reliably prompt is the investment in rules and examples. A works-once prompt has a role and a single instruction. It works for the first call and degrades from there. A works-reliably prompt has explicit rules for every known failure mode and concrete examples that anchor the output format.
   856|
   857|I spend about an hour per week on prompt maintenance. I review the logs from the previous week, identify patterns in agent failures, and update the rules or examples for the affected prompts. This is not prompt engineering. It is editing. I am making the instructions clearer based on where the agent went wrong.
   858|
   859|The single biggest improvement I made to our prompts was removing ambiguity. I replaced "be thorough" with "call the enrichment tool and the scoring tool for every lead." I replaced "be careful with pricing" with "never include pricing in the first email." I replaced "prioritize high-value leads" with "score each lead 1-5 based on company size and message intent."
   860|
   861|Clear instructions produce reliable agents. Vague instructions produce unreliable agents that occasionally get lucky. The second generation of our prompts was half the length of the first and twice as effective. Brevity forces precision.

   863|## Chapter 18 — Testing Without Breaking
   864|
   865|I deployed an agent to production that immediately sent a hundred emails to the wrong people. Not test emails. Real emails. To real customers. With wrong information.
   866|
   867|It was a reporting agent. It was supposed to send weekly summaries to department heads. I had tested it in a sandbox. It worked perfectly. I promoted it to production. The first batch went to the wrong email list. The agent read the distribution list from our CRM, but it read the internal field name instead of the email field. Every department head got someone else's report.
   868|
   869|The mistake was mine. I did not test with production data. I tested with mock data where the email field and the name field happened to have the same values. The agent looked correct in the sandbox and wrong in reality.
   870|
   871|That incident cost me a day of apologizing and a system I call three-stage testing. I have used it for every agent since. No failures in production for over six months.
   872|
   873|Stage one is safe testing. The agent runs in a fully isolated environment. It has no access to real tools, real data, or real APIs. Every tool call returns mock data. You can test as aggressively as you want without consequences.
   874|
   875|Our safe environment is a separate database with synthetic records. Fake customers, fake emails, fake orders. The agent processes these and produces outputs. I check whether the outputs are structurally correct. Does the lead responder produce the right JSON format? Does the logistics coordinator call the right tools in the right order? Does the contract reviewer flag the right clauses?
   876|
   877|Safe testing catches format errors, tool call errors, and prompt parsing errors. It does not catch logic errors because the mock data is too clean. Real data is messy. Mock data is tidy. A prompt that works perfectly on tidy mock data can collapse on the first real input with a missing field.
   878|
   879|Stage two is correct testing. The agent runs in a staging environment that mirrors production. It has access to real tools but operates on a copy of the data. The staging database is a snapshot from the previous week. The email API is set to a test mode that captures all outbound messages without delivering them. The CRM is a sandbox instance with copied records.
   880|
   881|Correct testing answers two questions. Does the agent make the right decision given real data? Does the agent produce the right output for a human to review?
   882|
   883|I run stage two for at least fifty agent runs before moving to stage three. Fifty runs is enough to hit the common edge cases. Missing fields. Duplicate records. Unusual formatting. Special characters. Every time the agent fails in stage two, I fix the prompt or add a rule before restarting the count.
   884|
   885|One example. During correct testing of the lead responder, the agent received a lead with a company name that included a trademark symbol. The enrichment tool could not find the company because the symbol was in the query. The agent returned a partial profile and scored the lead based on incomplete data. We added a rule to strip special characters from company names before calling the enrichment tool. Problem solved in stage two, never seen in production.
   886|
   887|Stage three is useful testing. The agent runs in production but with a human watchdog. Every output is reviewed before any action is taken. No automated sends. No automated updates. The agent works, but a human gates every output.
   888|
   889|Stage three lasts one week. Seven days of production data, real conditions, human oversight. I look for two things. First, does the agent produce useful output that passes human review at least ninety percent of the time? Second, does the agent handle the unexpected inputs that did not appear in stage two?
   890|
   891|The first week of useful testing for the lead responder revealed a problem we had missed. The agent handled English leads well. Spanish leads produced lower quality outputs. The score was often wrong because the agent could not assess the intent from the translated message. We added a language detection step. If the lead message is not in English, the agent flags it for manual handling and skips scoring. That rule went in during the useful testing week.
   892|
   893|The staging pattern is the infrastructure that enables this testing. We have three environments. Dev is for safe testing. Staging is for correct testing. Prod is for useful testing. Each environment is identical in code and different in data access and tool permissions.
   894|
   895|Dev uses mock APIs. All tool calls return fake data. The agent can call any tool without consequences.
   896|
   897|Staging uses real APIs with sandbox credentials. The CRM sandbox. The email test mode. The calendar test tenant. The data is real but the effects are contained.
   898|
   899|Prod uses real APIs with production credentials but with human approval gates. The agent can suggest anything, but nothing executes without a human saying yes.

   917|## Chapter 19 — Monitoring: How to Know It's Working
   918|
   919|I had an agent running for three weeks before I realized it was failing half the time. The agent was supposed to check shipment statuses and flag delays. It was running, it was logging, it was generating outputs. No one complained. No alerts fired. But when I finally looked at the data, forty-seven percent of the tool calls were failing silently.
   920|
   921|The shipping API had changed its response format. The agent expected a field called "estimated_delivery." The API now returned "eta." Every call succeeded at the HTTP level and returned a 200 status code. But the agent's enrichment step received null for the delivery date because the field name did not match. The agent logged "No data found" and moved on. No error. No alert. No human noticed for three weeks.
   922|
   923|That is the monitoring problem. Agents look like they are working when they are not. They do not crash. They produce output. The output is just wrong. You need visibility into what the agent is actually doing, not just that it is running.
   924|
   925|I now track four categories of metrics for every agent. Volume, accuracy, cost, and latency. Each category answers a specific question about agent health.
   926|
   927|Volume metrics answer the question: is the agent doing the work? I track runs per hour, runs per agent, and runs by outcome category. Outcome categories are completed, failed, escalated, and rejected. Completed means the agent finished its workflow. Failed means the agent hit an error it could not recover from. Escalated means the agent handed off to a human. Rejected means a human rejected the agent's output.
   928|
   929|The volume dashboard shows a bar chart for the last seven days. Each day has four colored bars for the four outcomes. If the failed bar starts growing, something is broken. If the rejected bar grows, the prompt needs updating. If the completed bar stays flat while lead volume increases, the agent is bottlenecked.
   930|
   931|Accuracy metrics answer the question: is the agent doing the work correctly? I track human approval rate, correction rate, and error rate. Approval rate is the percentage of agent outputs that pass human review without changes. Correction rate is the percentage that need edits before approval. Error rate is the percentage that are rejected entirely.
   932|
   933|The lead responder's approval rate is ninety-three percent. The correction rate is five percent. The error rate is two percent. Those numbers have been stable for four months. If approval rate drops below eighty-five percent, I pause the agent and investigate.
   934|
   935|Accuracy metrics are the most important because they are the only direct measure of agent quality. Volume metrics tell you the agent is busy. Accuracy metrics tell you the agent is useful.
   936|
   937|Cost metrics answer the question: is the agent worth running? I track cost per run, cost by tool, and cost by model. Cost per run is the total token cost divided by the number of completed runs. Cost by tool shows which tool calls are eating the most tokens. Cost by model shows which models are cheapest for which tasks.
   938|
   939|The average cost per lead responder run is two point three cents. The average cost per logistics coordinator run is four point one cents. The average cost per contract reviewer run is eight point two cents. If the cost per run spikes, something changed. Maybe the model increased prices. Maybe the agent is making more tool calls than expected. Maybe the context window is growing.
   940|
   941|I set cost alerts at two times the average. If any agent exceeds twice its normal cost per run for a full day, I get a notification.
   942|
   943|Latency metrics answer the question: is the agent fast enough? I track end-to-end run time, per-tool latency, and queue wait time. End-to-end is how long a complete agent run takes from input to output. Per-tool latency is how long each tool call takes. Queue wait time is how long outputs sit before human review.
   944|
   945|The lead responder completes in an average of eight seconds. The logistics coordinator averages fourteen seconds. The contract reviewer averages forty-five seconds because it uses a slower, more capable model. If the lead responder takes more than fifteen seconds, something is wrong. Probably a slow API call or a context window that grew too large.
   946|
   947|My dashboard is a single Grafana page. Four rows of panels, one row per metric category. Each row has a sparkline for the last thirty days and a current value. Red, yellow, green thresholds are set for each metric. Green is normal. Yellow means investigate. Red means act.
   948|
   949|The dashboard auto-refreshes every sixty seconds. I check it twice a day. Morning coffee and end of day. Each check takes about thirty seconds. I scan for red panels first, then yellow, then glance at the trends.
   950|
   951|The most important panel is the one that shows the last twenty-four hours of failed runs with their error messages. This panel is my early warning system. If I see a new error message, I investigate immediately. Most errors are transient. API timeouts, rate limits, network blips. But a new error message is often the first sign of a real problem.
   952|
   953|I learned to watch for patterns, not individual failures. One failed run is noise. Five failed runs with the same error in an hour is a signal. My dashboard flags patterns automatically. If the same error appears more than three times in an hour, the panel turns yellow.
   954|
   955|The logging infrastructure behind the dashboard is straightforward. Every agent run produces a structured log entry. Tool calls, decisions, outcomes, timestamps, costs. The logs go to a central database. The database powers the dashboard queries. The whole stack costs about fifty dollars per month in hosting.
   956|
   957|The alternative is no monitoring, which is what I had for the first three months. I thought the agent was working. It was not. I thought I would notice if something went wrong. I did not.   1032|## Chapter 21 — Multi-Agent Architecture
  1033|

  1041|
  1042|The lead capture part needs speed and breadth. Grab any form submission, any email, any LinkedIn message, and stuff it into the pipeline. Don't overthink it. The monitoring part needs patience.
  1043|
  1044|These are different skills. Different priorities. Different failure modes.

  1047|
  1048|The fix is specialization. You don't hire one person to run your entire business. You hire a salesperson, a marketer, an operations person, a customer support person. Each has a focused role. Each knows what they're responsible for. Each has tools specific to their job.
  1049|
  1050|Agents work the same way.

  1059|

  1079|## Chapter 22 — The Orchestrator Pattern
  1080|
  1081|The three-agent system worked better than the monolith. But I still had a problem. Who routes the work? When the capture agent finds a lead, how does it know the qualification agent is ready? What happens when the qualification agent is busy with another lead? What if the outreach agent crashes while sending an email?
  1082|
  1083|I needed a traffic cop. Someone who delegates, monitors, and handles exceptions. That's the orchestrator.
  1084|
  1085|The orchestrator pattern is simple on paper. One supervisor agent that doesn't do actual work. Instead, it receives requests, decides which worker agent should handle them, passes the work along, and waits for the result. If the worker fails, the orchestrator retries or escalates. If the worker succeeds, the orchestrator decides what happens next.
  1086|
  1087|Think of it like a project manager who doesn't code, doesn't design, doesn't write copy. The PM just makes sure the right person gets the right task at the right time. That's the orchestrator.
  1088|
  1089|I built mine using a pattern I call the router loop. The orchestrator runs in a continuous loop. Each cycle, it checks the incoming queue for new work. If there's work, it reads the task, checks its type, and routes it to the appropriate worker. Then it stores the result and checks for the next task. The loop repeats every few seconds.
  1090|
  1091|The workers don't talk to each other. They don't know the other agents exist. The capture agent outputs a lead record and forgets about it. The qualification agent picks it up from the queue, processes it, and outputs a scored lead. The outreach agent picks the scored lead and handles the communication. The orchestrator manages the handoffs.
  1092|
  1093|This is how Hermes Agent works under the hood. Hermes has a supervisor that receives a user's request . "check my email, find anything urgent, draft replies" — and breaks it into subtasks. Check email is one subtask. Evaluate urgency is another. Draft replies is a third. The supervisor dispatches each subtask to a specialized worker, collects the results, and assembles the final response.
  1094|
  1095|The key insight is that the orchestrator doesn't need to be smart. It needs to be reliable. The smart work happens in the workers. The orchestrator just needs to route correctly, handle timeouts, and manage retries. A simple loop with a switch statement handles most of it.
  1096|
  1097|Here's what my orchestrator looks like in practice:
  1098|
  1099|The capture agent finds a new lead and pushes it to the new-leads queue. The orchestrator polls this queue every five seconds. When it finds a new entry, it creates a task record with a unique ID, the lead data, and a status of "pending." It assigns the task to the qualification agent and updates the status to "processing."

If the lead is hot, it creates a new task for the outreach agent. If warm, it schedules a task for the nurture sequence. If cold, it archives the lead.
  1102|
  1103|This pattern handled every edge case I threw at it. The capture agent goes down? The orchestrator keeps polling, and the work queues up. The qualification agent takes too long? The orchestrator has a timeout . if a task stays in "processing" for more than 60 seconds, it retries with a fresh worker instance. The outreach agent fails mid-email? The orchestrator catches the error, logs it, and puts the task back in the queue for retry.
  1104|
  1105|The timeout and retry logic was the hardest part to get right. Early on, I set the timeout too short. The qualification agent sometimes took 45 seconds on a complex lead with lots of research.   1106|
  1107|The other thing I learned: the orchestrator needs a dead letter queue. When a task fails three times, it goes to a special queue that I review manually. Not everything can be automated. Some leads are genuinely confusing. Some data formats are broken. Some worker agents crash for reasons that need human investigation. The dead letter queue catches these and flags them for my attention. I check it once a day.
  1108|
  1109|The orchestrator also handles scaling. When I had one capture agent and one qualification agent, the system worked fine for 10 leads a day. When I hit 30 leads a day, the qualification agent became the bottleneck. It took 30 seconds per lead, so 30 leads meant 15 minutes of processing time. The orchestrator handled this by spinning up a second qualification agent instance. Two workers processing in parallel cut the time in half.
  1110|
  1111|I didn't have to rewrite any code. The orchestrator just added another worker to the pool and distributed tasks between them. The workers don't care how many peers they have. They just read from the queue and write results.
  1112|
  1113|The orchestrator pattern isn't new. It's how any distributed system works. But applying it to AI agents changed everything for me. Instead of one agent struggling to do everything, I had a system that could grow, recover from failures, and handle variable load without breaking.
  1114|
  1115|The cost went up . I was running more models simultaneously. But the reliability went up more. I stopped waking up to failed pipelines. I stopped losing leads because an agent got confused. The orchestrator absorbed all the chaos and presented a clean interface.
  1116|
  1117|If you build a multi-agent system, start with the orchestrator. Not the workers. Build the loop, the queues, the timeout logic, the retry mechanism, the dead letter queue. Get that right first. Then add workers one at a time. The workers are replaceable. The orchestrator is the backbone.
  1118|
  1119|I spent two weeks on the orchestrator before I added a second worker. It felt like wasted time. It wasn't. Every failure I've had since then was handled by the orchestrator, not by me.

  1121|## Chapter 23 — Pipelines: Data That Flows Between Agents
  1122|
  1123|My first multi-agent setup had a problem. The capture agent found a lead and passed it to the qualification agent. But the qualification agent kept asking the same questions. Company name? Industry? Where'd this lead come from? The capture agent had already captured that information. Why was the qualifier starting from scratch?
  1124|
  1125|Because I hadn't defined the interface between them.
  1126|
  1127|Pipelines aren't just about moving data from point A to point B. They're about defining what data moves, what format it's in, and what happens when the data doesn't match expectations. A pipeline is a contract between agents. The capture agent agrees to output a specific structure. The qualification agent agrees to accept that structure and augment it.
  1128|
  1129|My MIFECO pipeline has five stages: capture, qualify, contact, track, report. Each stage has an input schema and an output schema. The capture agent outputs a lead record with fields for company name, contact name, email, source, timestamp, and the original message. The qualification agent reads those fields, adds its own . score, confidence, industry fit, recommended action — and passes the augmented record along.
  1130|
  1131|The contract makes the system predictable. If the capture agent can't produce a valid record, it doesn't send it. It logs an error and tries again. If the qualification agent receives a record missing required fields, it rejects it and the orchestrator routes it to a repair handler.
  1132|
  1133|The repair handler was something I added after the first week of production. A lead came in through LinkedIn, and the capture agent couldn't extract an email address. It output the record anyway, with the email field as null. The qualification agent tried to research the company and couldn't find a contact. The pipeline stalled.
  1134|
  1135|I wrote a repair handler that intercepts records with missing critical fields. It tries to find the missing data . web search, social media lookup, email pattern guessing. If it finds what it needs, it fills in the gaps and sends the record back to the pipeline. If it can't find anything after three tries, it flags the record for manual review.
  1136|
  1137|The repair handler became a permanent part of the architecture. About 8% of inbound leads need some kind of repair. Usually a missing email or a company name that's too vague to research. The handler fixes about half of those automatically. The other half go to my manual review queue.
  1138|
  1139|The biggest lesson I learned about pipelines is that data quality degrades at every handoff. Each time data moves from one agent to another, something gets lost. A field gets misinterpreted. A date format changes. A status code gets dropped. The further data travels from its source, the more errors accumulate.
  1140|
  1141|I measure data loss at every handoff. The capture stage starts with 100% of the original data. After the qualification stage adds its fields, I check: does the record still have the original email? The original timestamp? The original message text? If any of those are missing or corrupted, I have a pipeline bug.
  1142|
  1143|This saved me more than once. Early on, I noticed that the qualification agent was truncating the original message field to 500 characters. My capture agent captured the full message, sometimes thousands of characters. The qualifier used a model with a smaller context window and clipped the input. The outreach agent was writing follow-up emails based on the first 500 characters of the original inquiry, missing the part where the prospect asked a specific question.
  1144|
  1145|I fixed it by changing the pipeline schema. The original message stays in a separate field that the qualifier passes through unchanged. The qualifier only reads it, never writes it. Pass-through fields became standard practice after that.
  1146|
  1147|Mid-pipeline failures are the hardest to handle. A lead makes it through capture and qualification. It's scored as hot. The orchestrator routes it to the outreach agent. The outreach agent starts drafting an email. Halfway through, the API call to the email service fails. The email is half-written. The pipeline is stuck.
  1148|
  1149|My solution was transactional handoffs. Each stage either completes fully or rolls back. The outreach agent doesn't mark a lead as "contacted" until the email is sent and confirmed by the email service. If the API fails, the lead stays in "outreach pending" status. The orchestrator picks it up on the next cycle and retries.
  1150|
  1151|The transactional approach means I sometimes send duplicate emails. The email service confirms the send, but the confirmation gets lost in transit. The outreach agent doesn't see the confirmation and sends the email again. This happened three times before I added a dedup layer at the email service level. Now the service checks for duplicate content before sending.
  1152|
  1153|I track pipeline velocity as my primary health metric. How long does a lead take to move from capture to qualification? From qualification to first contact? From first contact to meeting booked? Each stage has a target time. Capture to qualification: under 30 seconds. Qualification to first contact: under 5 minutes. First contact to meeting: depends on response time, but I track the median.
  1154|
  1155|When velocity drops, something is wrong. The qualification agent might be overloaded. The outreach agent might be hitting rate limits. The email service might be degraded. The pipeline metrics tell me where to look.
  1156|
  1157|The pipeline pattern works because it forces structure. You can't have five agents working together without defining what each one produces and consumes. The act of designing the pipeline schema reveals assumptions that would otherwise stay hidden. The capture agent assumed email was always present. The qualifier assumed timestamps were in UTC. The outreach agent assumed the prospect's name was in a specific field. Writing the interface exposed all these mismatches before they caused production failures.
  1158|
  1159|If you're building a multi-agent system, start with the pipeline. Define the schema first. Write the contract before you write the agents. It's not exciting work. But neither is debugging a corrupted lead record at 11 PM on a Sunday.
  1160|
  1161|The last thing I'll say about pipelines is that they're never finished. New lead sources appear. Existing sources change their data formats. The business adds new qualification criteria. Each change means updating the schema, the handoffs, or the repair handlers. The pipeline is a living system, not a static design. I review it quarterly and find something to improve every time.

  1163|## Chapter 24 — Agents That Work While You Sleep
  1164|
  1165|I was asleep when the deal closed. 2:47 AM. A prospect from three weeks ago . a manufacturing company in Ohio — filled out the contact form, got qualified, received a personalized proposal, and signed the contract. All while I was dreaming about whatever I dream about.

An email that bounced without a retry.

It archives leads that have been cold for more than 90 days. It refreshes Company House data for active prospects.

The maintenance agent found them, merged them into one record, and preserved all the notes. I'd been looking at fragmented data for weeks without realizing it.
  1184|
  1185|Optimization tasks run weekly. They analyze pipeline performance and suggest improvements. Which lead sources produce the best prospects? Which outreach messages get the best response rates? What time of day gets the most engagement? The optimization agent runs these analyses every Sunday morning and generates a report.
  1186|
  1187|The optimization report changed my outreach strategy. The agent noticed that leads from LinkedIn had a 40% higher close rate than leads from web forms. But my capture agent was treating them identically. I adjusted the qualification criteria to weight LinkedIn leads higher. Close rate went up 12% in the first month.
  1188|
  1189|Scheduling these tasks took trial and error. The first version ran everything at midnight. Monitoring, maintenance, optimization . all at once. The agents competed for model capacity.   1190|
  1191|I staggered the schedules. Monitoring runs hourly, every hour. Maintenance runs at 2 AM, when traffic is lowest. Optimization runs at 6 AM Sunday, when the week's data is complete. Each task has its own budget allocation and its own queue. No conflict.
  1192|
  1193|The hardest part was designing tasks that run correctly when I'm not there to supervise. A reactive agent has a direct cause and effect: lead arrives, agent processes. A proactive agent has to make assumptions about what the system needs at 3 AM when no one is watching.
  1194|
  1195|The maintenance agent's archive logic had a bug in the first version. It archived leads that were cold for 90 days . meaning no contact in 90 days. But it didn't check whether those leads had an active email thread. A lead that went cold but had just replied to an old email got archived anyway. I lost three conversations before I noticed.
  1196|
  1197|The fix was a check: don't archive any lead with activity in the last 7 days, regardless of the 90-day cold rule. Activity includes emails, form submissions, website visits, anything. If the lead is doing something, the lead is alive.
  1198|
  1199|Proactive agents also need to handle partial failures gracefully. When the monitoring agent runs at 3 AM and the database connection fails, what happens? My first version crashed and the monitoring skipped that hour. I missed a stalled lead for 9 hours because of a transient database error.
  1200|
  1201|Now every scheduled task has retry logic and a notification escalation. If a task fails once, it retries in 5 minutes. If it fails three times, the task is logged and I get a notification. The notification doesn't wake me up . it's queued for my morning summary. But it's recorded.
  1202|
  1203|The next day I check the error log, fix the issue, and re-run the failed tasks. Usually it's a rate limit or a temporary API outage. Rarely a real bug.
  1204|
  1205|The agents that work while I sleep have changed my business more than the reactive agents. Reactive agents save me time during the day. Proactive agents save me from problems I didn't know existed. They catch the leaks, fix the gaps, and optimize the system . all without asking for permission.
  1206|
  1207|I still check the pipeline every morning. But the proactive agents have eliminated most of the surprises. When I open my dashboard at 7 AM, I already know what happened overnight. The monitoring agent told me.
  1208|
  1209|## Chapter 25 — Deduplication and Data Quality
  1210|
  1211|I ran a pipeline health check three months in. The results stopped me cold. 23% of my lead records were duplicates. Nearly a quarter of my database was useless noise.
  1212|
  1213|The capture agent was doing its job . too well. It found leads from web forms, LinkedIn, email inquiries, event signups, and referrals. But the same person showing up from different sources became different records. Jane Smith from Acme Corp filled out a web form on Monday. Jane Smith from Acme Corp emailed me on Wednesday. Jane Smith from Acme Corp registered for a webinar on Friday. Three records. One human.
  1214|
  1215|The qualification agent scored each one separately. The outreach agent sent three different emails to the same person. The prospect got three variations of "thanks for your interest" from the same company in the same week. They wrote back: "Are you guys okay over there?"
  1216|
  1217|This is the garbage in, garbage out problem. Every agent system ingests data. If that data is dirty, every agent downstream makes bad decisions. The deduplication problem isn't glamorous. It isn't AI. It's data cleaning. But if you skip it, your agents will embarrass you.
  1218|
  1219|The dedup problem in lead generation is harder than it looks. Exact matches are easy . same email address, same company, same name. But real-world data is messy. Jane Smith and J. Smith might be the same person. Acme Corp and Acme Corporation might be the same company. jane@acme.com and jane.smith@acme.com might be the same inbox. The system needs fuzzy matching.
  1220|
  1221|I tried several approaches before finding one that worked. The first attempt was simple string comparison: if the email domain matched and the company name was similar, flag it as a potential duplicate. This caught the obvious cases but missed a lot. Company names in particular were inconsistent. "Acme Manufacturing Co." and "Acme Manufacturing Company" are the same entity but a string comparison sees a difference.
  1222|
  1223|The second attempt used a similarity scoring approach. Each record gets compared to existing records using a weighted score. Email exact match: 40 points. Company name similarity: 25 points. Contact name similarity: 20 points. Domain match: 15 points. Records scoring above 70 are merged automatically. Records between 50 and 70 are flagged for review.
  1224|
  1225|This worked better but had a problem. The weights were arbitrary. Some duplicates scored 80 when they weren't actually duplicates . two different people at the same company. Others scored 55 when they were clearly duplicates — same person, slightly different spelling.
  1226|
  1227|The third attempt used the agent itself. I wrote a dedup agent that takes a new lead and compares it against recent records. It reads both records and makes a judgment: are these the same person? Same company? Should they be merged? The agent explains its reasoning and assigns a confidence score.
  1228|
  1229|The agent approach caught matches the fuzzy scoring missed. It recognized that "Bob" is short for "Robert." It knew that "jane@acme.com" and "jane.smith@acme.com" on the same day, same company, same phone number were the same person. It could read the original message content and see that both inquiries were about the same product.
  1230|
  1231|But the agent approach was slow. Each dedup check took 10-15 seconds and cost a fraction of a cent. With 30 new leads a day and checking against 500 existing records, the dedup agent ran 15,000 comparisons. That's expensive and slow.
  1232|
  1233|The final solution was a hybrid. The fuzzy matcher runs first as a fast filter. It catches exact and near-exact matches in under a second. Anything the fuzzy matcher flags above 60 confidence goes straight to merge. Anything below 40 confidence is assumed unique. The middle zone . 40 to 60 confidence — goes to the dedup agent for judgment.
  1234|
  1235|The hybrid approach handles about 70% of cases with the fast filter, 15% with the agent, and leaves 15% as uncertain. The uncertain ones get tagged "potential duplicate" and wait for my weekly review. Most of those I confirm as duplicates in about 5 seconds. The agent could handle them too, but the cost-benefit isn't there for the edge cases.
  1236|
  1237|Data quality goes beyond dedup. I also check for invalid emails, bounced addresses, bad phone numbers, and stale records. The validation pipeline runs every new record through a series of checks before it enters the main pipeline.
  1238|
  1239|Email validation is the most important. About 4% of inbound leads have typos in their email addresses. jane@gmil.com instead of gmail. b0b@company instead of bob. The email validation agent checks the format, pings the MX record, and flags suspicious patterns. Flagged emails get a gentle correction request rather than a bounced outreach attempt.
  1240|
  1241|The tools I use are simple. For fuzzy matching, I use a library called RapidFuzz . it's fast and handles the common cases. For email validation, I use a combination of regex patterns and DNS lookups. For name normalization, I have a lookup table of common nicknames and abbreviations. Nothing fancy. Just consistent application of basic rules.
  1242|
  1243|The most important practice is measuring data quality over time. I track duplicate rate, invalid email rate, and completeness score for every lead source. Web forms have a 98% completeness rate but a 5% invalid email rate. LinkedIn leads have 100% email accuracy but only 60% completeness . missing phone numbers and company size. The data tells me which sources need more validation and which need more enrichment.
  1244|
  1245|The duplication rate dropped from 23% to 3% after implementing the hybrid dedup system. That means 20% more of my database is usable. The outreach agent stopped sending embarrassing duplicate messages. The qualification agent scored leads based on complete, unique records. The pipeline became trustworthy.
  1246|
  1247|Data quality isn't an AI problem. It's an operations problem. Your agents will amplify whatever data you feed them. Clean data means clean decisions. Dirty data means dirty outcomes. The tools exist. The patterns are known. You just have to prioritize it.
  1248|
  1249|I spent more time on dedup and data quality than I spent on any single agent. That felt wrong at first. The agents are the exciting part. The data cleaning is the boring part. But the boring part is what keeps the exciting part from embarrassing you. Every hour I spent on data quality saved me ten hours of debugging agent behavior caused by bad data.
  1250|
  1251|## Chapter 26 — When Agents Fail
  1252|
  1253|The email went out at 10:34 AM. Subject line: "Your Invoice . Payment Overdue." Body: a stern reminder that the account was past due. It was addressed to my biggest customer.
  1254|
  1255|It was also completely wrong. The customer had paid three days ago. The payment was sitting in my bank account. But the monitoring agent didn't check the bank account. It checked the invoice system, which had a sync delay. The agent saw an unpaid invoice and sent the collection notice automatically.
  1256|
  1257|The customer called me at 10:37 AM. "What the hell is this?"
  1258|
  1259|I apologized, refunded a month of service, and learned the hardest lesson about agent systems: they will fail, and when they fail, they fail fast and at scale. One human making an embarrassing mistake is awkward. One agent making the same mistake is a system sending 47 incorrect collection notices before you notice the bug.
  1260|
  1261|Graceful degradation is the practice of designing failures so they cause minimum damage. The system shouldn't crash. It should slow down, skip non-critical tasks, and alert the right person. Graceful degradation is the difference between a system that fails safely and one that sets your biggest customer on fire.
  1262|
  1263|My first attempt at graceful degradation was naive. I wrote error handlers that caught exceptions and logged them. If an agent failed, it retried twice. If it failed again, it stopped and notified me. That handled the technical failures . API timeouts, database connection errors, rate limits. But it didn't handle the semantic failures. The agent that sent the wrong email didn't throw an exception. It succeeded at doing the wrong thing.
  1264|
  1265|Semantic failures need different handling. The system needs to check not just whether an action succeeded, but whether it was the right action to take. This is harder because it requires understanding the business context, not just the technical result.
  1266|
  1267|I added a confirmation agent. Before the outreach agent sends any email, the confirmation agent reviews it. The confirmation agent isn't smart . it's a rules engine with a language model. It checks for red flags: words like "overdue" and "final notice" and "collections." It checks whether the lead stage matches the email type — don't send a proposal to an unqualified lead. It checks whether the prospect has replied recently — don't send a follow-up to someone who just said "not interested."
  1268|
  1269|The confirmation agent catches about 80% of the semantic errors. The remaining 20% need human review. I built a queue for these . flagged messages that the confirmation agent couldn't confidently approve. I review the queue once in the morning and once in the afternoon.
  1270|
  1271|The retry logic for technical failures went through three versions. Version one retried immediately. Bad idea. If the database is down, retrying immediately will fail again. The retries just hammer the already-failing service.
  1272|
  1273|Version two used exponential backoff. First retry after 5 seconds. Second after 25 seconds. Third after 125 seconds. This worked better but had a problem . the pipeline stalled during long backoffs. A lead that needed outreach sat in the queue for 2 minutes while the retry timer counted down.
  1274|
  1275|Version three uses a circuit breaker. After two consecutive failures to a service, the circuit opens and all calls to that service fail fast for 30 seconds. No retries, no waiting. The orchestrator routes around the failing service if possible. If the email API is down, the outreach agent writes the email and saves it to a pending queue. The email goes out when the API comes back. The pipeline doesn't stall.
  1276|
  1277|The dead letter queue is where unprocessable work goes to die. A lead with a corrupt data format. A task that failed its maximum retries. A request that violates business rules. Instead of crashing the pipeline, these items go to the DLQ. I check it daily.
  1278|
  1279|The DLQ taught me things about my system I wouldn't have learned otherwise. The most common item in the DLQ is leads from sources I haven't configured the capture agent to handle. A referral from a partner that comes in an unexpected format. A form submission from a test environment that slipped through. These aren't failures. They're signals that my pipeline has gaps.
  1280|
  1281|I catalog every DLQ item and review the pattern quarterly. If the same issue appears three times, I fix the pipeline to handle it. Over six months, the DLQ volume dropped from 5 items a week to less than 1. The system learned to handle edge cases I didn't know existed.
  1282|
  1283|The escalation chain is manual by design. If the capture agent fails to process a lead, the orchestrator retries. If it fails three times, the lead goes to the DLQ. I get a daily digest of DLQ items. If the same capture agent fails more than five times in an hour, I get an immediate notification. That's a genuine system problem, not an edge case.
  1284|
  1285|I learned to distinguish between failures I should fix and failures I should tolerate. A 1% failure rate on email sending is acceptable. Email services have transient issues. The retry logic handles most of them. A 1% failure rate on lead capture is not acceptable. Every lead is potential revenue. The capture agent needs to be more reliable than the email agent.
  1286|
  1287|The collection notice disaster cost me a month of revenue from my biggest customer. But it also forced me to build the confirmation agent, the circuit breaker, and the escalation chain. Those systems have prevented worse disasters since. The customer forgave me. They're still a customer.
  1288|
  1289|Agents fail. That's the nature of building systems that interact with the real world. The question isn't whether they'll fail. The question is whether you'll catch it before it matters.
  1290|
  1291|The collection notice incident changed how I think about failure. I used to optimize for preventing failures. Now I optimize for detecting them early. The prevention is important, but I can't predict every way the system will break. What I can do is make sure the system tells me when it breaks, and that the damage is contained while I fix it.
  1292|
  1293|## Chapter 27 — Scaling: From 10 Leads to 100
  1294|
  1295|When I built the first pipeline, I designed it for 10 leads a day. That felt generous. I was getting maybe 5. The system ran smoothly for two months. Then I published a blog post that got some traction. The next week, I got 47 leads in one day. The week after that, 82. By the third week, I was averaging 60 leads a day, and the pipeline was on fire.
  1296|
  1297|The capture agent handled the volume fine. It was just writing records. The qualification agent started choking. Each lead took 30 seconds to evaluate. 60 leads meant 30 minutes of processing time. The qualification queue grew faster than the agent could empty it.
  1298|
  1299|The queues were the first bottleneck. I watched the dashboard as the pending-queue count climbed. 12. 24. 38. 52. Leads that arrived at 9 AM weren't getting qualified until 11 PM. The outreach agent was idle because there was nothing to contact. The leads that got contacted the next day were 12 hours old . response rates drop dramatically after the first hour.
