{"content": "  1301|I added more qualification agents. Two instances running in parallel cut the queue time in half. Four instances cut it to a quarter. But each instance cost money. Four qualification agents running simultaneously meant four model API calls. My costs tripled in a week.
  1302|
  1303|The rate limits hit next. The model provider had a per-minute limit on API calls. Four qualification agents making simultaneous calls hit that limit in the first 15 minutes. Requests started getting 429 errors. The retry logic kicked in, which made the queue backup worse. Now agents were spending time waiting for retries instead of processing leads.
  1304|
  1305|I solved the rate limit problem by staggering the workers. Instead of four agents running continuously, I set a concurrency limit of two. When the queue backed up beyond 20 items, a third worker activated. When it dropped below 10, the third worker deactivated. The system scaled dynamically based on demand.
  1306|
  1307|The dynamic scaling worked because the orchestrator already had queue monitoring. It was a small change to add worker scaling logic. The orchestrator checks queue depth every 30 seconds. If depth exceeds threshold, it spins up additional workers. If depth drops below threshold, it spins them down. The workers are stateless containers, so starting and stopping is clean.
  1308|
  1309|Cost became the next problem. Each qualification run costs about 2 cents with the mid-tier model I was using. 60 leads a day meant $1.20 in qualification costs. 200 leads a day would mean $4.00. That's manageable. But the outreach agent used a top-tier model at 8 cents per run. The monitoring agent ran every hour. The maintenance agent ran daily. The optimization agent ran weekly. The costs added up.
  1310|
  1311|I looked at the cost breakdown and found something surprising. The monitoring agent was the most expensive component. It ran every hour, checked every active lead, and generated a summary. Each check cost 1 cent. With 200 active leads, that's $2.00 per run. 24 runs per day. $48 per day on monitoring alone. More than I was spending on qualifying leads.
  1312|
  1313|I redesigned the monitoring agent. Instead of checking every lead every hour, it checked leads by priority. Hot leads got checked every 15 minutes. Warm leads every hour. Cold leads every 4 hours. The monitoring cost dropped from $48 to $12 per day. Alert quality improved because high-priority leads got more attention.
  1314|
  1315|Alert fatigue was the hidden problem. When the system was handling 10 leads a day, every alert felt important. When it handled 100 leads a day, the same alert frequency would have driven me insane. A 1% error rate on 10 leads is nothing. A 1% error rate on 100 leads means something breaks every day.
  1316|
  1317|I redesigned the alert system around thresholds. Individual errors get logged but not alerted. Alerts fire when the error rate exceeds 2% in an hour, or when a queue backs up beyond 50 items, or when no leads have been processed in 30 minutes. These thresholds filter out the noise and signal the real problems.
  1318|
  1319|Model quality degradation appeared at scale too. The qualification agent worked great on the first 500 leads. It scored accurately, caught spam, and identified good prospects. Around lead 800, I noticed the quality slipping. The agent was approving leads that should have been rejected. It was scoring inconsistent.
  1320|
  1321|The problem was context drift. The agent's instructions referenced examples from the first 500 leads, which were mostly from my network. As the lead sources diversified . different industries, different company sizes, different countries — the examples became less relevant. The agent was calibrated for a lead profile that no longer matched reality.
  1322|
  1323|I updated the qualifications instructions quarterly. Each update uses the last 90 days of data to generate new examples. The agent sees fresh examples of good leads, bad leads, and edge cases. Qualification accuracy recovered after each update.
  1324|
  1325|Scaling from 10 to 100 leads taught me that the system that works at small scale is different from the system that works at medium scale. The bottlenecks shift. The costs compound. The alerts multiply. You can't just run the same system faster. You have to redesign for the new volume.
  1326|
  1327|The dynamic scaling, cost optimization, and alert redesign took about two weeks of work. The system handles 150 leads a day now without breaking a sweat. The costs are predictable. The alerts are meaningful. The pipeline runs without constant intervention.
  1328|
  1329|I don't know where the next bottleneck is. But I know there is one. Scaling reveals problems that don't exist at smaller volumes. The trick isn't eliminating all bottlenecks. It's staying ahead of the next one.
  1330|
  1331|The pipeline handles 150 leads a day now. At some point it'll handle 500. At that volume, the dynamic scaling will hit new limits . model provider concurrency caps, database write throughput, queue processing latency. I don't know what the next bottleneck will be. But I'm watching for it.
  1332|
  1333|## Chapter 28 — Security and Access Control
  1334|
  1335|The qualification agent had access to my CRM. That was the mistake.
  1336|
  1337|It made sense at the time. The agent needed to look up existing contacts, check deal stages, and update records. So I gave it API credentials with write access to the CRM. The agent used those credentials for thousands of successful operations. Then one day, it found a lead that confused it.
  1338|
  1339|The lead was from a company that matched one of my existing customers. Same name, same industry, similar website. The qualification agent couldn't decide if it was a new prospect or an existing account. It tried to resolve the ambiguity by creating a new contact record . then a new account — then merging the two. The merge operation failed because the accounts were linked to active deals. The agent retried. And retried. And retried.
  1340|
  1341|I came back from lunch to 47 notifications from my CRM. The agent had created 17 duplicate contact records, initiated 12 merge operations, and locked 3 accounts. The CRM admin had to untangle the mess.
  1342|
  1343|This is the principle of least privilege applied to autonomous systems. Give an agent the minimum access it needs to do its job. Not the access you think it needs. Not the access that's convenient. The minimum.
  1344|
  1345|My agents now have strict access boundaries. The capture agent can write to the new-leads database but cannot read the CRM. It doesn't need to know about existing customers. It just needs to store what it captures. The qualification agent can read the CRM and the new-leads database. It can write scores and notes to the lead record. It cannot create, delete, or merge records. Those actions require human approval.
  1346|
  1347|The outreach agent is the most restricted. It can read lead records and write to the communications log. It cannot modify lead status. It cannot access customer payment data. It cannot send emails to any address outside the approved lead list. The agent has a strict allowed-sender policy . it can only use the outreach email address I configured. If the agent tries to send from a different address, the email service rejects it.
  1348|
  1349|The access boundaries are enforced at the API level, not at the agent level. The agent doesn't decide whether it can perform an action. The API does. The agent requests an action, and the API checks the permission. If the permission is denied, the action fails and the agent logs the failure. The agent can't override the API security.
  1350|
  1351|This saved me from a worse incident. A monitoring agent had scheduled a database cleanup that would have deleted old lead records. The agent sent the delete request to the API. The API checked the agent's permissions. Delete was not in its allowed actions. The API returned a permission denied error. The agent logged the failure. I reviewed it the next morning and disabled that cleanup task.
  1352|
  1353|The scary stories aren't hypothetical. One of my agent configurations accidentally sent a follow-up email to a prospect's CEO instead of the original contact. The agent had confused the contact hierarchy. It found the CEO's email through a web search and included both contacts on the reply. The CEO wrote back asking why his subordinate was being contacted about a deal he knew nothing about. I lost that deal.
  1354|
  1355|The fix was a contact restriction. The outreach agent can only send to the primary contact on a lead record. It cannot add secondary contacts without explicit approval. The agent can suggest secondary contacts in its notes, but the email action requires a confirmed recipient list.
  1356|
  1357|I also learned to compartmentalize agent identities. Each agent has its own API key with its own permissions. If one agent is compromised . through a prompt injection or a corrupted instruction — the damage is contained. The capture agent's API key can't access the CRM. The qualification agent's key can't send emails. The outreach agent's key can't modify databases. A breach in one agent doesn't cascade to others.
  1358|
  1359|The compartmentalization also makes auditing easier. Every action is logged with the agent's identity. I can see which agent captured which lead, which agent scored it, which agent sent which email. If something goes wrong, I have a clear chain of custody. The logs tell me exactly which agent did what and when.
  1360|
  1361|Guardrails are the next layer. The qualification agent has a rule: never score a lead above 90 confidence without a second opinion. If the agent is highly confident, it still needs the confirmation agent to verify. This catches overconfident mistakes. The outreach agent has a rule: never send more than 5 emails to a single prospect in a 7-day period. The monitoring agent enforces this rule across all agents. If the outreach agent hits the limit, the monitoring agent blocks the action.
  1362|
  1363|The guardrails are simple rules written in plain language. No complex policy engine. No AI-driven access control. Just clear, hard limits that the system enforces. "Never send email to a contact who has replied with the words 'not interested'." "Never modify a deal that has a status of 'closed won'." "Never capture a lead from an email address that has unsubscribed."
  1364|
  1365|These rules catch the most common failure patterns. They don't catch everything. But they catch the expensive mistakes.
  1366|
  1367|The CRM incident taught me that convenience is the enemy of security. I gave that agent write access to the CRM because it was faster than setting up proper permissions. I paid for that decision with hours of cleanup work. The principle of least privilege sounds bureaucratic. But when your agents run unsupervised, the restrictions are what keep them from causing real damage.
  1368|
  1369|I review agent permissions every month. Each agent gets a permission list. I check each permission against the agent's actual job. If the agent doesn't need a permission, I revoke it. The lists get shorter over time, not longer. That's the goal. Less access means less surface area for mistakes.
  1370|
  1371|The autonomous enterprise runs on trust, but not blind trust. The agents are trusted to act within their boundaries. The boundaries are the safety net.
  1372|
  1373|## Chapter 29 — Cost Management
  1374|
  1375|People ask me what this costs. The honest answer: about $380 a month for the MIFECO agent system. That covers model API calls, email service, CRM integration, and the infrastructure to run it all. $380 a month to handle 100+ leads, qualify them, send personalized outreach, and manage the pipeline.
  1376|
  1377|The breakdown matters. Not because the total is impressive, but because the decisions behind the numbers tell you how to think about cost.
  1378|
  1379|The biggest expense is model API calls at $210 per month. That's the language models that power the agents. Not one model. A mix of models, each chosen for a specific job. The capture agent uses a cheap model . about $0.15 per million input tokens. The qualification agent uses a mid-tier model at $0.50 per million tokens. The outreach agent uses a premium model at $2.50 per million tokens.
  1380|
  1381|Different jobs need different models. The capture agent just extracts text from forms and emails. A cheap model handles that perfectly. The qualification agent needs judgment . it evaluates company fit, lead quality, and intent. The mid-tier model handles this well enough. The outreach agent writes messages that represent my company. Tone matters. Premium model here.
  1382|
  1383|This is the cheap model plus expensive model strategy. Use the cheapest model that can do the job. Reserve expensive models for tasks where quality directly impacts revenue. Don't use GPT-4o to extract form data. Don't use a cheap model to write a proposal that a prospect will read.
  1384|
  1385|The strategy saved me from a cost spiral. My first version used the premium model for everything. It worked well. It also cost $1,200 a month. When I split the tasks by model, the cost dropped 70% with no noticeable quality change for the lower-tier tasks.
  1386|
  1387|Caching cut costs further. The qualification agent often evaluates leads from the same companies. If I've already researched Acme Corp, the cache returns the result without making another API call. The cache hit rate is about 30% . three out of ten qualification requests are duplicates. That's $15 a month saved.
  1388|
  1389|The cache has a 24-hour expiry. Company information changes. A company that was small last week might have grown. A lead's job title might have changed. The cache refreshes daily. The trade-off between cache staleness and cost savings is worth it.
  1390|
  1391|Batching is the other cost lever. The monitoring agent, which checks the pipeline every hour, used to make one API call per check. That's 24 calls a day. I batched the checks into a single call that evaluates the entire pipeline state. One call instead of 24. The cost dropped from $12 per day to $1.50. The quality didn't change because the batched request had more context.
  1392|
  1393|The fallback chain is my favorite cost optimization. The outreach agent tries the premium model first. If it's rate-limited or returns an error, it falls back to the mid-tier model. If that fails too, it falls back to the cheap model. The fallback chain runs silently. The agent gets the job done regardless of which model handled it.
  1394|
  1395|About 5% of outreach tasks fall back to the mid-tier model. Less than 1% fall to the cheap model. The fallback saves me from failed outreach when the premium model has an outage or rate limit issue. It also cuts costs because I set aggressive rate limits on the premium model . it runs cheaper when usage is throttled.
  1396|
  1397|The model selection decision framework is simple. Three questions for each task. Is this task visible to customers? If yes, use the premium model. Is this task making a decision that affects revenue? If yes, use the mid-tier at minimum. Is this task purely mechanical . data extraction, record keeping, format conversion? Use the cheap model.
  1398|
  1399|The framework isn't perfect. Some tasks straddle the lines. The confirmation agent reviews customer-facing messages before they go out. It's not customer-facing itself, but its errors lead to customer-facing problems. I use the mid-tier model for the confirmation agent. It's good enough to catch the major issues and costs half what the premium model would.
  1400|
  1401|Monthly infrastructure cost is $95. A small VPS runs the orchestrator, the queues, and the database. The pipeline processing happens on this server. It's a standard Linux box with 4GB of RAM. Nothing special. The agents don't run locally . they run through API calls to model providers. The server just coordinates the workflow.
  1402|
  1403|Email service costs $45 per month. CRM costs $30 per month. Monitoring and logging cost $15 per month. Total: $380.
  1404|
  1405|The revenue generated by the system is harder to pin down because attribution is messy. But I know that before the agent system, I responded to about 40% of inbound leads within 24 hours.   1475|## Chapter 31 — The Four Pillars
  1476|
  1477|I used to think the right way to build an agent system was to plan everything up front. Map out every process. Document every workflow. Then build it all at once. That approach nearly killed MIFECO's agent project before it got started. We spent three months designing a system that would automate everything end-to-end. We built nothing. We shipped nothing.   1478|

  1480|
  1481|The four-pillar framework saved us. I didn't invent it. I stole it from watching how the business actually worked and then giving it a name so I could explain it to my team.   1482|
  1483|Pipeline is revenue. This is every activity that brings money in the door. Lead generation, outreach, qualification, follow-up, pipeline management, proposal generation.   1484|
  1485|Operations is fulfillment. This is everything that happens after the sale. Order processing, project management, resource allocation, scheduling, delivery tracking. You cannot start with operations first because you have nothing to fulfill.
  1486|
  1487|Support is retention. This is the work that keeps customers happy after delivery. Ticket triage, FAQ responses, escalation routing, satisfaction monitoring, renewal tracking.   1488|
  1489|Intelligence is strategy. This is the layer that makes everything smarter. Data analysis, pattern detection, alerting, forecasting, recommendation generation.   1490|
  1491|The dependency chain is simple. Pipeline pays for everything. You automate revenue first because revenue funds the rest.   1499|The pattern repeats. Automation at MIFECO followed the money. Every agent we built had to justify its existence in terms of either generating revenue, reducing cost, or protecting retention. If it didn't do one of those three things, we didn't build it.

  1509|
  1510|## Chapter 32 — Agents Talking to Agents
  1511|
  1512|The first time two of my agents tried to talk to each other, they nearly deleted an entire week of scheduled meetings. I had built them independently. A scheduler agent that booked meetings with prospects. A fulfillment agent that assigned resources to confirmed engagements. They worked fine alone. Then I connected them and watched chaos unfold.
  1513|
  1514|The scheduler agent sent a confirmation to a prospect and simultaneously notified the fulfillment agent to assign a resource. The fulfillment agent received the notification, assigned a project manager to the slot, and sent a confirmation back to the scheduler agent. The scheduler agent, not programmed to ignore internal confirmations, interpreted the fulfillment agent's message as a new prospect inquiry and started a fresh scheduling workflow for the same person. The two agents ping-ponged for four minutes before I noticed. They generated seventeen duplicate calendar entries, sent five identical confirmation emails to the prospect, and locked up the project manager's calendar with phantom bookings.
  1515|
  1516|That was the day I learned that agents talking to agents is not a convenience. It is a hazard.
  1517|
  1518|The fundamental problem is that each agent operates with incomplete context. The scheduler agent knew about prospect availability and meeting requests. It had no concept of resource allocation. The fulfillment agent knew about resource capacity and assignment rules. It had no concept of why a meeting was scheduled. When they communicated, each interpreted the other's output through its own limited frame of reference. That is exactly how infinite loops start.
  1519|
  1520|I have identified three specific failure modes in inter-agent communication, and I have built specific solutions for each.
  1521|
  1522|The first failure mode is the infinite loop. Agent A sends data to Agent B. Agent B processes it and sends something back to Agent A. Agent A processes the return and sends something back to Agent B again. This can run forever if nothing stops it. At MIFECO, every agent now has a hard timeout limit on any conversation thread. If an inter-agent exchange exceeds five messages on the same thread, the exchange terminates and both agents flag the issue to the supervisor agent. Five is an arbitrary number. I picked it because it caught my seventeen-duplicate disaster. You should pick a number that makes sense for your workflows. The important thing is that the limit exists and it stops loops cold.
  1523|
  1524|The second failure mode is conflicting instructions. Agent A tells the CRM to update a contact status to "qualified." Agent B tells the CRM to update the same contact status to "disqualified" because its scoring algorithm disagrees. Neither knows the other exists. At MIFECO, we solved this with priority hierarchies. Every agent has a priority level. Pipeline agents have higher priority than fulfillment agents because if pipeline and fulfillment disagree about whether a deal is real, pipeline's assessment wins. You cannot fulfill a deal that should not have been a deal in the first place. When two agents of equal priority conflict, neither writes. The conflict is escalated to a human operator. I review it and decide. That happens about once a week.
  1525|
  1526|The third failure mode is circular dependency. Agent A cannot complete its task without data from Agent B. Agent B cannot complete its task without data from Agent A. Both sit idle waiting for the other. This happened at MIFECO with our proposal generation agent and our pricing agent. The proposal agent needed pricing data to generate a quote. The pricing agent needed a proposal scope to calculate pricing. They deadlocked. I solved this with a supervisor arbitration layer. A third agent, the supervisor, detects when an agent has been waiting more than fifteen minutes for data from another agent. The supervisor breaks the deadlock by providing default values from a static table, logging the event, and alerting me. The default values are conservative. They protect the business while a human sorts out the configuration error. The deadlock is always a configuration error.
  1527|
  1528|The protocols that make inter-agent communication possible are not magic. They are boring infrastructure that matters enormously. At MIFECO, we use a combination of three approaches.
  1529|
  1530|First, MCP — the Model Context Protocol. This is a standardized way for agents to declare what tools they offer and what data they need. It is not a product. It is a specification. Think of it as a contract format. Agent A publishes: "I offer scheduling services. I need: contact name, email, preferred time range." Agent B reads that and knows exactly what to send. Without MCP, agents use ad-hoc formats and every integration is a fragile custom parser. I have broken many integrations that way.
  1531|
  1532|Second, webhooks for event-driven communication. When a pipeline agent qualifies a lead, it fires a webhook that the scheduling agent subscribes to. The scheduling agent does not poll. It does not check a database every minute. It receives a notification when there is something to do. This reduces latency and computation cost. At MIFECO, our average inter-agent notification delay is under two seconds.
  1533|
  1534|Third, shared state for complex workflows. Some tasks require multiple agents to coordinate over time. A deal that moves through qualification, scheduling, proposal, and fulfillment involves four agents across three days. Each agent needs to know what the previous agents decided. We use a shared workflow state object stored in our database. Each agent reads the state, does its work, and writes its output back. The supervisor agent monitors the state for anomalies. If a deal sits in the same state for more than twenty-four hours, the supervisor alerts me.
  1535|
  1536|The most important lesson I can give you about inter-agent communication is this: build agents that work alone first. Connect them only after each is proven reliable independently. If you connect two unreliable agents, you get an exponential mess. I learned this the hard way with the duplicate meeting disaster.
  1537|
  1538|Test inter-agent handoffs with a human in the loop initially. Let the human approve or reject each transfer before the receiving agent acts on it. This slows things down but it prevents catastrophic cascades. Once you trust the handoffs, remove the human from the loop one handoff at a time. I still keep human approval on the handoff between proposal generation and fulfillment. That is the point where real money changes hands, and I want a human's eyes on it.
  1539|
  1540|The protocols are not the interesting part. The discipline is. Clear contracts, strict limits, priority rules, supervisor oversight. These are not technical decisions. They are operational decisions about how you want your business to run.

  1580|## Chapter 34 — When Not to Use Agents
  1581|
  1582|I run over thirty agents at MIFECO. They handle lead generation, prospect research, email outreach, meeting scheduling, pipeline tracking, project monitoring, status reporting, data analysis, and customer triage. They work 24 hours a day. They never take vacation. They never call in sick. They handle thousands of tasks per week that I used to do by hand.
  1583|
  1584|But there are things I still do myself. Every single one. And there are things no agent at MIFECO will ever do, no matter how good the technology gets.
  1585|
  1586|Let me be honest about the boundaries.
  1587|
  1588|The first category is relationship building. Real relationship building. Not the transactional kind where you send a birthday email or check in after a purchase. The kind where you sit with a prospect who is struggling with a problem and listen. Not to collect data. Not to identify their needs so you can pitch. To listen because you care. An agent cannot do that. An agent can simulate listening. It can ask follow-up questions. It can reference previous conversations. But it cannot actually care. And the other person knows. I have tested this. I have let agents handle entire introductory conversations with prospects and then asked those prospects afterward if they noticed anything unusual. Some did not. But the ones who became long-term partners noticed. They could feel the difference. They described it as "something off" or "too scripted" or "like talking to a sales manual." Those are the relationships I want. Those are the ones I handle personally.
  1589|
  1590|At MIFECO, I personally take every partner call. A partner call is a conversation with someone who has agreed to a strategic relationship, not a transaction. I handle the first introduction with any prospect who fits our highest-value customer profile. The agents handle the volume. I handle the relationships that matter most. That split has kept our close rate on high-value deals above sixty percent while the agents handle the broad pipeline.
  1591|
  1592|The second category is creative strategy. Not tactical strategy. That is fine for agents. "Send follow-up three days after no reply" is a tactical decision an agent can make. But creative strategy — the kind that asks "what market should we enter next" or "how should we reposition our offering" or "what message will resonate with an audience we have never reached before" — that requires synthesis of disparate information, intuition, and the kind of pattern recognition that comes from lived experience. Agents can analyze data. They cannot have intuition. They can summarize competitor moves. They cannot feel the market shift. I have tried to delegate strategic thinking to agents. The results were bland. Safe. Obvious. The kind of strategy a committee produces. Nobody wins with obvious strategy.
  1593|
  1594|The third category is negotiation. Genuine negotiation. Not price negotiation on a standard deal. That is a set of rules. "Give ten percent discount on annual contracts. No discount below twenty percent margin." An agent can execute those rules. But negotiating a partnership structure, a co-marketing arrangement, a resource trade, or a custom deal that has no precedent — that requires reading the other person, knowing when to push and when to yield, and understanding what the other party values that they have not said. Agents cannot read unspoken signals. They cannot sense when silence means hesitation versus when silence means contemplation. I have seen agents push too hard on prospects who were nearly ready to sign. I have seen agents yield too quickly on terms that mattered. I do not let agents negotiate anything beyond standard pricing.
  1595|
  1596|The fourth category is judgment calls with no right answer. Should we invest in this new market or double down on our existing one? Should we hire another engineer or another salesperson? Should we pivot our product or iterate on what we have? These questions have no objective answer. They have consequences and probabilities, but no ground truth. Agents are terrible at these because they optimize for what can be measured. They will tell you to double down on your existing market because the data exists there. They will tell you to hire more salespeople because the ROI is more certain than engineering. They will tell you to iterate because new products are risky. These are defensible answers. They are also usually wrong when the business needs to grow. I make these calls myself. I use agent-provided data to inform them. I do not delegate the decision itself.
  1597|
  1598|The fifth category is anything requiring genuine empathy. A customer whose project failed. A partner whose expectations were not met. An employee who is struggling. An agent can send a nice message. It can express sympathy. It can even customize the message based on context. But it does not feel anything and the recipient knows. I have received automated sympathy messages. They do not help. At MIFECO, every escalation from a dissatisfied customer routes to a human. Every failed project triggers a personal call from me or a senior team member. Every partner complaint gets a same-day human response. The agents triage. The humans heal.
  1599|
  1600|Here is what I still do myself at MIFECO. I take every partner introduction call. I review and edit every major proposal before it goes out. I make all hiring and firing decisions. I make all strategic direction decisions. I handle all customer escalation calls. I personally call any prospect who reaches the proposal stage without responding to agent outreach. Those calls convert at about forty percent. The agents did the groundwork. I close.
  1601|
  1602|And there is one more thing. I still mess with the system. I change agent configurations directly. I rewrite prompts. I adjust thresholds. I test new approaches on live data. The agents do not manage themselves yet. I doubt they ever will completely. That is the work I find most interesting. It is the work I refuse to automate.
  1603|
  1604|If you are building an agent system, ask yourself honestly what should never be delegated. Write that list. Protect it. The temptation to automate everything is strong, especially when things are working well. But the things that make your business worth doing are the things only humans can do well. Do not automate those away.

  1607|## Chapter 35 — The AI Disclosure Question
  1608|
  1609|I got the question from a prospect six months into running agents. He had just finished a great conversation with our system. Three emails back and forth. A meeting booked. Everything smooth. Then he asked: "Was I talking to a human?"
  1610|
  1611|I told him the truth. The first two emails were generated by an agent. The third was a hybrid — the agent drafted it, I reviewed and edited it. The meeting was scheduled automatically. He paused for a moment. Then he said: "Okay. That makes sense. It was a little too responsive."
  1612|
  1613|He still took the meeting. He still became a customer. He still refers business to us. That moment shaped my approach to disclosure.
  1614|
  1615|The legal landscape around AI disclosure as of 2026 is fragmented. The European Union's AI Act requires disclosure when interacting with an AI system in most commercial contexts, unless it is obvious from the circumstances. California has introduced similar requirements through its AI Transparency Act. Several other states are considering bills. There is no single federal standard in the United States. Canada requires disclosure for automated decision systems that impact individuals. Japan has guidelines that recommend disclosure but do not mandate it. The patchwork is real and it is getting more complex, not less.
  1616|
  1617|But here is what I have found in practice. Most customers do not care that an agent contacted them. They care about the quality of the communication. If the message is relevant, timely, and useful, they do not ask whether it came from a human or an agent. If the message is irrelevant, poorly timed, or useless, they do not care that a human wrote it. They are still annoyed.
  1618|
  1619|At MIFECO, I took a specific approach to disclosure. I decided to be transparent about automated outreach upfront. Our cold emails include a line at the bottom: "This outreach is powered by our AI agent system, but a human reviews every reply." That is true. I do review every reply. The line is simple, direct, and honest. It has not reduced our response rate. In fact, it might have increased it. Some prospects have replied specifically because they were curious about the agent system.
  1620|
  1621|For inbound conversations — prospects who reach out to us first — we do not proactively disclose unless asked. If someone fills out a contact form on our website, the initial response is generated by an agent. Most people never notice. The ones who do notice usually ask. I tell them honestly. Nobody has walked away because of it.
  1622|
  1623|For ongoing customer interactions, the disclosure is simpler. Our support agents identify themselves as automated in the first response. "This is an automated response to your inquiry. If you need human assistance, reply with ESCALATE." Most customers do not escalate. They get the answer they need and move on. The customers who escalate get a human response within fifteen minutes. That works.
  1624|
  1625|Here is what I have learned about the real risks. The risk is not that customers will discover you use agents. The risk is that your agents behave badly. A misconfigured agent that sends aggressive follow-ups, makes promises it cannot keep, or provides incorrect information creates far more damage than any disclosure policy could prevent. I have had two agent incidents that damaged customer relationships. Both were behavior problems, not disclosure problems. One agent sent seven follow-ups to the same prospect in twenty-four hours because a configuration error multiplied the sequence count. The prospect was furious. I apologized personally. He stayed a customer but it took months to rebuild trust. Disclosure was not the issue. Behavior was.
  1626|
  1627|The second risk is consistency. If you disclose in one context but not another, you create the appearance of deception. At MIFECO, we use a consistent approach across all channels. Email, chat, phone transcription, all have the same disclosure standards. If a prospect asks on a phone call whether they are talking to an agent, we tell them. The agents are trained to answer honestly if asked.
  1628|
  1629|The third risk is legal, but it varies by jurisdiction. I am not a lawyer. I consulted one when designing our disclosure approach. The advice I received was simple: disclose when required by law in your jurisdiction and your customer's jurisdiction. Be honest if asked. Do not hide the use of agents. That advice has served us well.
  1630|
  1631|What about employees? I tell my team everything about the agents. They know what each agent does, how it makes decisions, what its limitations are. This is not altruism. It is practical necessity. My team members need to know when to trust an agent's output and when to override it. They cannot do that if they do not understand how the agent works. Every new hire gets a walkthrough of the agent system. They can see the prompts. They can see the configurations. They can see the failure logs. Transparency inside the company has prevented dozens of operational mistakes.
  1632|
  1633|What about partners? We disclose agent usage in our partnership agreements. The language is simple: "MIFECO uses automated systems for lead generation, communication, and workflow management. These systems operate under human supervision." No partner has objected. Most are doing the same thing themselves.
  1634|
  1635|The honest truth is that the disclosure question is overblown in most discussions. It matters legally in certain jurisdictions. It matters ethically as a matter of principle. But in practical business terms, what matters far more is whether your agents work well. A transparent bad agent is still bad. A quiet good agent is still good.
  1636|
  1637|I have had exactly one customer who asked detailed questions about our agent system and then decided not to work with us because of it. One. In two years. That is a rounding error in our pipeline. Meanwhile, I have had dozens of customers who worked with us for months before realizing agents were involved. They did not care when they found out. The work was good. That was all that mattered.
  1638|
  1639|Focus on making your agents behave well. Disclose appropriately for your jurisdiction and customer base. Be honest when asked. And spend more time worrying about whether your agents are sending seven follow-up emails than about whether you told someone an agent sent the first one.

  1641|## Chapter 36 — Building an Agent-First Culture
  1642|
  1643|The first person whose job I automated at MIFECO was myself. I built an agent to handle prospect research. That freed up about ten hours a week that I had been spending on manual data gathering. I used those hours to build more agents. The second person I affected was our salesperson. The agents started handling initial outreach. She stopped sending cold emails. She started working only with prospects who had already expressed interest. She did not lose her job. Her job changed. She made more commission because she spent her time closing instead of prospecting.
  1644|
  1645|That was the easy one. The harder transitions came later.
  1646|
  1647|When I automated project status reporting, our operations manager felt threatened. She had been doing those reports manually for two years. They were part of her routine. They were tedious, but they were hers. I did not handle the transition well. I built the agent, turned it on, and told her the reports would now be generated automatically. She was quiet. Two weeks later she told me she felt like her role was being hollowed out. She was right. Her role was being hollowed out. What I should have done was show her what she could do with the time saved before I took the reports away.
  1648|
  1649|I learned from that mistake. Every automation since has followed a different pattern. I identify what the agent will take over. I identify what the person will gain. I build both changes before making either. The person does not lose a task and then look for something to fill the gap. The person loses a task and immediately gains a more valuable one.
  1650|
  1651|The jobs that emerge in an agent-first company are not the jobs anyone talks about at conferences. They are concrete, operational, and necessary.
  1652|
  1653|Agent trainers are the people who build and maintain the agents. They write the prompts. They configure the workflows. They set the thresholds. They test changes in staging environments before deploying to production. At MIFECO, this is a hybrid role. Our best agent trainer is a former sales operations person who understood the workflow before she understood the technology. She learned the technical side in about a month. She was effective immediately because she knew what the agents should do. Technical skill was secondary to domain knowledge.
  1654|
  1655|Exception handlers are the people who deal with what the agents cannot handle. Every agent has edge cases. A prospect with a non-standard request. A project that does not fit the template. A customer whose situation does not match any rule. These exceptions get routed to a human. The exception handler resolves them and logs the resolution so the agent can be improved. At MIFECO, our customer-facing team members are exception handlers by default. They handle the escalations. They process the anomalies. They feed the learnings back to the agent trainer. This role requires judgment, adaptability, and comfort with ambiguity. It is a better job than sending the same emails every day.
  1656|
  1657|System operators are the people who watch the dashboard, respond to alerts, and keep the agents running. They handle the daily volume and error checks I described in chapter 33. They restart agents that have failed. They investigate anomaly spikes. They manage the supervisor arbitration layer. At MIFECO, this role rotates among the technical team. Everyone spends a week per month on system operator duty. It builds shared understanding of how the system works and shared ownership of its failures.
  1658|
  1659|The transition period is hard. I will not pretend otherwise. When you automate someone's work, they feel loss. They feel threat. Some of those feelings are irrational. Some are entirely rational because their job may genuinely need to change. The only honest approach is to be direct about what is happening and what it means for them.
  1660|
  1661|At MIFECO, I told my team: "The agents will handle volume. You will handle relationships. The volume work is what nobody enjoys anyway. The relationship work is what makes this company special. I am automating the boring parts so you can focus on the parts that matter." That framing worked for most people. A few did not want the change. They wanted to keep doing what they were doing. I helped two team members transition to other roles outside MIFECO. That was the right thing to do. They were not bad employees. They just did not want the job that was emerging.
  1662|
  1663|The people who thrived were the ones who saw the agents as tools rather than threats. Our salesperson who stopped cold prospecting and started closing high-value deals doubled her income in six months. Our operations manager who stopped writing reports and started designing better workflows became our most valuable non-technical contributor. Our support person who stopped answering the same five questions every day and started handling complex escalations reported higher job satisfaction after three months.
  1664|
  1665|The culture shift is not about convincing everyone to love automation. It is about making the new work clearly better than the old work. If your agents make people's jobs worse, they will resist. If your agents make people's jobs better by removing drudgery and enabling higher-value work, they will adapt.
  1666|
  1667|One specific practice that helped at MIFECO: I include the team in agent design. When I plan a new agent, I ask the people whose work it will touch what the agent should do and what it should not do. They know the edge cases I have never encountered. They know the exceptions that do not fit the rules. They have saved me from building at least three agents that would have caused more problems than they solved. Involving the team early also reduces resistance. Nobody fights a tool they helped design.
  1668|
  1669|The goal is not to replace people. The goal is to replace tasks so people can do better work. That sounds like a slogan. It is not. It is the operational reality of how MIFECO runs. The agents handle the work nobody wants to do. The humans handle the work only humans can do. That arrangement works only if the humans trust the agents and the agents are built by the humans.

  1671|## Chapter 37 — The Roadmap: Year One
  1672|
  1673|Let me give you a month-by-month plan. This is not aspirational. This is exactly what I would do if I were starting from scratch today, knowing everything I know now. I have built this system from zero agents to over thirty. I have made every mistake on this path. The roadmap below skips the mistakes and shows the direct route.
  1674|
  1675|Month 1: Pick one task. Build one agent. The task must meet three criteria. It is a task you do at least once a week. It follows rules, not judgment. It has a measurable outcome. For MIFECO, that first task was prospect research. Find companies in a target industry. Find decision-makers at those companies. Verify their email addresses. Output a spreadsheet. That was it. One agent. One task. I spent about forty hours building and testing it. The deliverable for month 1 is a working agent that performs one task better than you did it manually. Not faster. Better. If it is not better, fix it or scrap it.
  1676|
  1677|Month 2: Measure and iterate. You now have one agent running. You need data. Track how many tasks it completes per day. Track the error rate. Track the output quality compared to your manual work. At MIFECO, our first agent produced six qualified leads in its first week. Manual research would have produced three or four. The agent was already better. But I found issues. It missed companies that used certain website platforms. It returned incorrect email formats for some industries. I spent month 2 fixing those issues. The deliverable for month 2 is a reliable agent with tracked performance metrics and a lower error rate than month 1.
  1678|
  1679|Month 3: Add a second agent. Pick a task that connects to the first one. If your first agent researched prospects, your second agent should contact them. At MIFECO, agent two was an outreach agent. It took the output of agent one and sent personalized cold emails. The connection between the two agents was the prospect data file. Agent one wrote to it. Agent two read from it. No real-time handoff. Just a shared data source. Month 3 is about getting two agents to coexist without conflict. The deliverable is two independent agents that work on related parts of the same workflow without breaking each other.
  1680|
  1681|Month 4: Interconnect them. Now build the handoff. Agent one completes a prospect. Agent two receives a notification and begins outreach. At MIFECO, this was a webhook. Agent one fired an event. Agent two subscribed to it. The handoff took two days to implement and a week to stabilize. Problems emerged. Duplicate notifications. Timing issues. Prospect data that arrived incomplete because agent one had not finished writing. I solved each problem as it appeared. Month 4's deliverable is two agents that pass work between them reliably.
  1682|
  1683|Month 5-6: Pipeline automation. Expand from two agents to a complete pipeline workflow. At MIFECO, months five and six added a qualifier agent that analyzed replies and scored buying intent, a scheduler agent that proposed meeting times, and a CRM update agent that logged every interaction. By the end of month six, a prospect could be researched, contacted, engaged, qualified, and scheduled with no human touching the process. Deliverable: an end-to-end pipeline from prospect identification to meeting booked. Measure meetings per week, conversion rate, and cost per meeting.
  1684|
  1685|Month 7-8: Operations automation. Add the fulfillment side. At MIFECO, this meant agents that monitor project timelines, generate status reports, track deliverables, and flag overdue tasks. These agents do not generate revenue directly. They reduce the cost of delivery. Month seven is building the agents. Month eight is stabilizing them and training the team to trust them. Deliverable: operations agents running with error rates under two percent and at least one detected problem that was caught before it caused a customer impact.
  1686|
  1687|Month 9-10: Support automation. Add the retention layer. At MIFECO, this meant a support triage agent that processed incoming inquiries, answered routine questions from a knowledge base, and escalated complex issues to humans. Month nine builds the agent. Month ten tunes it based on actual customer interactions. Deliverable: a support agent handling at least fifty percent of incoming inquiries without human involvement, with customer satisfaction scores equal to or better than human-only support.
  1688|
  1689|Month 11-12: Optimization and intelligence. Build the monitoring and analysis layer. At MIFECO, this meant intelligence agents that tracked performance across all other agents, identified trends, detected anomalies, and generated recommendations. Month eleven builds the dashboards and alerting. Month twelve focuses on tuning thresholds and retiring any agent that does not justify its cost. Deliverable: a fully instrumented agent system with cost-per-task metrics, value attribution, and automated anomaly detection. At the end of year one, you should have a decision point. Either the system is generating measurable returns and you expand, or it is not and you audit honestly.
  1690|
  1691|The decision points are important. After month two, you know whether agents work for your business. If your first agent failed to improve over manual work, stop. Do not add more agents. Fix the approach or accept that your business may not be ready for this. After month six, you know whether pipeline automation pays. If your pipeline agents are generating less revenue than they cost, stop the expansion. Keep what works. Do not add operations or support until pipeline pays for them. After month twelve, you know whether you want to build a full autonomous system or operate with targeted automation in specific areas.
  1692|
  1693|MIFECO passed all three decision points. We kept expanding. But I have talked to business owners who stopped after month two because their first agent did not work well enough. That is fine. The roadmap works whether you go all the way or stop at a stable midpoint.
  1694|
  1695|The worst approach is skipping months. Do not jump to pipeline automation in month one. Do not interconnect agents you have not tested independently. Each month builds on the previous one. Skip a step and you will be debugging problems you could have prevented. I know because I skipped steps the first time and spent weeks untangling messes that a slower approach would have avoided entirely.
  1696|
  1697|Start with one agent. One task. This week. Not next quarter. Not when you have time. This week.

  1699|## Chapter 38 — Common Objections
  1700|
  1701|I have talked to hundreds of business owners about AI agents. I hear the same objections every time. Some are reasonable concerns. Some are excuses dressed as concerns. Here are the real answers to the real objections, based on actual operation, not marketing promises.
  1702|
  1703|Objection one: "It's too expensive." Let me give you real numbers. MIFECO runs over thirty agents. Our total monthly cost is roughly $380. That covers API calls, model inference, hosting, and infrastructure. Thirty agents. Three hundred and eighty dollars. The cheapest full-time employee in our company costs over four thousand dollars a month with benefits. One agent costs about what I spend on coffee. The math is not close.
  1704|
  1705|But the real cost is not the compute. The real cost is the time to build and maintain the agents. That is where the expense lives. My first agent took forty hours to build. That is about a week of focused work. If your time is worth one hundred dollars an hour, that agent cost you four thousand dollars to build. It better generate more than four thousand dollars in value before it needs significant rework. My first agent generated about twelve thousand dollars in attributed pipeline value in its first three months. The ROI was there. But it was not free. It cost time, attention, and iteration.
  1706|
  1707|If you are a small business owner with no technical background, you will need to either learn to build agents yourself or hire someone to do it. Both have costs. Learning takes time. Hiring costs money. Neither is trivial. But the return on a single good pipeline agent can exceed the investment within a quarter. Start small. Build one cheap agent. Measure its output. If the ROI is there, expand. If not, you have lost a few hundred dollars and some time. That is a manageable experiment.
  1708|
  1709|Objection two: "It's not reliable." This is fair. Agents fail. They fail in ways that are different from software failures. Software fails deterministically. Same input, same failure, every time. Agents fail probabilistically. They work fine for weeks and then suddenly misinterpret something and produce garbage output. I have seen this happen. An agent that processed prospect replies correctly for two months suddenly started classifying all replies as "interested" including unsubscribe requests. That cost us a week of cleanup.
  1710|
  1711|Here is the honest reliability data from MIFECO. Our pipeline agents have an uptime of 99.3 percent. That means they are running and responsive 99.3 percent of the time. But output quality is not the same as uptime. Output quality — the percentage of agent outputs that are correct and useful — runs around 94 percent across all agents. That means about six percent of agent outputs need human review or correction. The best agents hit 98 percent. The worst hit 87 percent.
  1712|
  1713|I handle this with two practices. First, every agent output goes through a validation step. A second agent or a validation rule checks the output before it reaches a customer. If validation fails, the output is blocked and flagged for human review. Second, I accept the six percent error rate as a cost of operation. It is cheaper to catch and correct those errors than to do all the work manually. But I do not pretend the errors do not exist. They do. You need processes to catch them.
  1714|
  1715|Objection three: "My customers won't like it." Most of your customers will not notice. I have run blind tests at MIFECO. We sent agent-generated communications to two hundred prospects without disclosure. Exactly seven asked whether they were talking to an automated system. The other one hundred ninety-three either did not notice or did not care enough to ask. Of the seven who asked, six proceeded after receiving an honest answer. One declined further contact. That is a 0.5 percent rejection rate.
  1716|
  1717|Your customers care about quality of communication, not source of communication. If your agent sends them relevant, useful, timely information, they will not care that it was generated automatically. If your agent sends them spam, irrelevant offers, or confusing messages, they will care regardless of whether a human wrote it.
  1718|
  1719|Objection four: "I don't know where to start." This is the easiest objection to solve. Pick one task. Not the most important task. Not the most strategic task. One task you do this week that is repetitive, rule-based, and measurable. Pick the task that irritates you the most. For me it was prospect research. For you it might be data entry, invoice generation, appointment confirmations, or status report writing. One task. Build one agent. That is where you start.
  1720|
  1721|The one-task rule solves analysis paralysis. It forces you to commit. You cannot build the perfect system on the first try. You can build one agent that does one thing adequately. That is enough to learn what works and what does not.
  1722|
  1723|Objection five: "I tried AI and it didn't work." This objection usually means one of two things. Either you tried a chatbot that was not an agent, or you tried to automate something too complex on the first attempt. A chatbot that answers FAQs is not an agent. An agent acts on your business systems. It sends emails. It updates your CRM. It books meetings. If you tried a chatbot that sat on your website and answered questions poorly, you did not try an agent. Try an agent.
  1724|
  1725|If you tried to automate your entire sales process in one month and it failed, the problem was scope, not technology. Break it down. Automate one step. Prove that step works. Automate the next. The roadmap in chapter 37 exists because I failed at the big-bang approach and succeeded with incremental builds. Start smaller than you think you need to.
  1726|
  1727|Objection six: "What if the agent makes a mistake that costs me money?" This is the real objection behind all the others. The answer is that agents will make mistakes that cost you money, and you will still come out ahead if you design the system correctly. At MIFECO, our agents have made mistakes that cost us approximately two thousand dollars total over two years. Mostly duplicate communications sent to prospects, incorrect data entered into CRM fields, and one scheduling mistake that double-booked a customer. The value generated by the agents during that same period is well into six figures. The mistake cost is noise.
  1728|
  1729|Mitigate mistakes with validation layers, human review on high-stakes outputs, and escalation paths for anomalies. But do not let the fear of mistakes stop you from starting. Your manual processes already have mistakes. You just do not measure them as carefully.

  1731|## Chapter 39 — Where Agents Are Going Next
  1732|
  1733|I am writing this in 2026. What I describe below will probably be outdated in two years. Some of it will be wrong within one. That is the nature of this space. It moves faster than any business book can track. But I have been inside this world for two years of production operation. I have a reasonably good sense of which coming changes are real and which are hype. Let me separate them.

The current quality is good enough for initial outreach, appointment reminders, and simple qualification. It is not good enough for negotiation, objection handling, or complex conversations. The voice quality has improved dramatically in the past year. The latency has dropped to near-human levels. The emotional range is still limited. A voice agent sounds professional and helpful. It does not sound warm and trustworthy. Yet.
  1736|
  1737|At MIFECO, I am experimenting with a voice agent for inbound customer support calls. Our pilot handles about thirty percent of incoming calls end-to-end. The customer identifies their issue, the agent looks up their account, provides status information or answers common questions. If the issue is complex, the agent transfers to a human with full conversation context. The initial results are promising. Average handle time dropped from eight minutes with a human to three minutes with the agent. Customer satisfaction is within five percent of human-only calls. I expect this number to improve.
  1738|
  1739|Video agents are further out. I have seen demos of asynchronous video communication where an agent generates a talking-head video responding to a customer's video inquiry. I do not think video agents will be production-ready for business communication within the next eighteen months. The risk of weird-looking outputs damaging brand perception is too high. Audio is fine. Text is fine. Video is not ready.
  1740|
  1741|Physical-world agents — drones, robots, automated equipment — are a different category entirely. These are not AI agents in the same sense. They are hardware systems with AI controllers. They matter for businesses that operate in the physical world. Warehouses, logistics, manufacturing, agriculture, construction. At MIFECO we have no physical operations, so I have no experience here. What I observe from peers in those industries is that physical automation is advancing steadily but slowly. Hardware iteration cycles are measured in years, not weeks. The AI controllers are getting smarter. The bodies are getting cheaper. But nobody should expect a drone delivery revolution within twelve months.
  1742|
  1743|The most significant infrastructure change coming is MCP standardization. The Model Context Protocol is the thing I am most excited about. Right now, building agents requires custom integrations for every tool. My agent that talks to Salesforce has a Salesforce-specific implementation. My agent that talks to HubSpot has a different one. Every integration is custom, fragile, and time-consuming. MCP is an attempt to create a universal protocol that any agent can use to interact with any tool. If a tool implements MCP and an agent implements MCP, they can talk without custom code.
  1744|
  1745|I think of MCP as the USB-C moment for AI agents. Before USB-C, every device had a different cable. You needed a drawer full of adapters. After USB-C, one cable works for almost everything. MCP aims to do the same for agent-tool communication. If it succeeds, building an agent that works with your CRM, your email system, your calendar, and your project management tool will take hours instead of weeks. The protocol is still early. Multiple implementations exist. They are not fully compatible yet. But the direction is clear and the momentum is strong. I am building new MIFECO agents with MCP support from day one.
  1746|
  1747|The agent app store is also coming. I have seen pitches for marketplaces where you buy pre-built agents like you buy software. A lead generation agent for real estate agents. A customer support agent for e-commerce stores. A project management agent for construction firms. Some of these exist already. Most are thinly wrapped GPT instances with a few preset prompts. The quality is inconsistent.
  1748|
  1749|I believe the agent app store will mature, but more slowly than the hype suggests. The problem is that agents are not software. Software does the same thing every time you run it. An agent adapts to your business, your data, your customers, your workflows. A pre-built agent that does not know your business is barely better than a generic chatbot. The successful agent marketplaces will be the ones that make customization easy, not the ones that offer the most agents. I am watching this space. I am not investing yet.
  1750|
  1751|What I am building next at MIFECO is a self-healing agent. An agent that monitors its own performance, detects when its output quality is degrading, and automatically retrains itself on recent successful examples. This is hard. It requires a feedback loop that measures output quality in real time, which most businesses do not have. But the need is real. Every agent I have built degrades over time. The market changes. The data sources change. The language patterns change. Manual retraining is my biggest ongoing maintenance cost. A self-healing agent would reduce that cost dramatically.
  1752|
  1753|The real changes in the next two years will not be dramatic breakthroughs. They will be boring infrastructure improvements. Better protocols. Better tooling. Better monitoring. Lower costs. The agents available today already work well enough to transform a business. The next wave will make them easier to build, easier to maintain, and harder to break. That is where the value is, not in some sci-fi vision of fully autonomous companies.
  1754|
  1755|Build now. The tools will get better. Your experience building with today's tools will be worth more than waiting for tomorrow's perfection.

name: browser
description: Direct browser control via CDP. Use when the user wants to automate, scrape, test, or interact with web pages. Connects to the user's already-running Chrome.
---

# browser-harness

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read install.md.

Domain skills (community-contributed per-site playbooks under `agent-workspace/domain-skills/`) are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `agent-workspace/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Headless Server Setup (Way 2 — no sudo, no X11)

When no desktop Chrome is available (common on cloud VPS / headless servers):

1. **Install Chromium via Playwright** (bundled, no sudo needed):
   ```bash
   npx playwright install chromium
   ```
   This installs to `~/.cache/ms-playwright/chromium-<ver>/chrome-linux64/chrome`

2. **Start Xvfb** for a virtual display:
   ```bash
   Xvfb :99 -screen 0 1920x1080x24  # background process
   ```

3. **Launch Chrome** with the debugging port and virtual display:
   ```bash
   DISPLAY=:99 ~/.cache/ms-playwright/chromium-<ver>/chrome-linux64/chrome \
     --remote-debugging-port=9222 \
     --user-data-dir=/tmp/chrome-bu \
     --no-first-run --no-default-browser-check \
     --disable-extensions --disable-gpu
   ```

4. **Set BU_CDP_URL** so browser-harness finds it:
   ```bash
   export BU_CDP_URL=http://127.0.0.1:9222
   ```

5. **Verify:**
   ```bash
   curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9222/json/version          # Browser + WebSocket info
   browser-harness -c 'print(page_info())'              # Connected and alive
   ```

## Listing All Tabs

Use raw CDP to enumerate all browser tabs:

```bash
browser-harness -c "
targets = cdp('Target.getTargets')
tabs = [t for t in targets.get('targetInfos', []) if t.get('type') == 'page']
for t in tabs:
    tid = (t.get('targetId','?') or '?')[:8]
    print(f'[{tid}] {t.get(\"title\",\"?\")}  --  {t.get(\"url\",\"?\")}')
print(f'Total: {len(tabs)} tab(s)')
"
```

Filter internal pages with `t.get("url","").startswith("chrome://")`.

## Usage

```bash
browser-harness -c '
new_tab("https://docs.browser-use.com")
wait_for_load()
print(page_info())
'
```

- Invoke as browser-harness — it's on $PATH. No cd, no uv run.
- First navigation is new_tab(url), not goto_url(url) — goto runs in the user's active tab and clobbers their work.

## Tool call shape

```bash
browser-harness -c '
# any python. helpers pre-imported. daemon auto-starts.
'
```

run.py calls ensure_daemon() before exec — you never start/stop manually unless you want to.

### Remote browsers

Use remote for parallel sub-agents (each gets its own isolated browser via a distinct BU_NAME) or on a headless server. BROWSER_USE_API_KEY must be set. start_remote_daemon, list_cloud_profiles, list_local_profiles, sync_local_profile are pre-imported.

```bash
browser-harness -c '
start_remote_daemon("work")                               # default — clean browser, no profile
# start_remote_daemon("work", profileName="my-work")      # reuse a cloud profile (already logged in)
# start_remote_daemon("work", profileId="<uuid>")         # same, but by UUID
# start_remote_daemon("work", proxyCountryCode="de", timeout=120)   # DE proxy, 2-hour timeout
# start_remote_daemon("work", proxyCountryCode=None)      # disable the Browser Use proxy
'

BU_NAME=work browser-harness -c '
new_tab("https://example.com")
print(page_info())
'
```

start_remote_daemon prints liveUrl and auto-opens it in the local browser (if a GUI is detected) so the user can watch along. Headless servers print only — share the URL with the user. The daemon PATCHes the cloud browser to stop on shutdown, which persists profile state. Running remote daemons bill until timeout.

Profiles (cookies-only login state) live in interaction-skills/profile-sync.md — covers list_cloud_profiles(), the chat-driven "which profile?" pattern, and sync_local_profile() for uploading a local Chrome profile.

## Interaction skills

If you start struggling with a specific mechanic while navigating, look in interaction-skills/ for helpers. They cover reusable UI mechanics like dialogs, tabs, dropdowns, iframes, and uploads. The available interaction skills are:
- connection.md
- cookies.md
- cross-origin-iframes.md
- dialogs.md
- downloads.md
- drag-and-drop.md
- dropdowns.md
- iframes.md
- network-requests.md
- print-as-pdf.md
- profile-sync.md
- screenshots.md
- scrolling.md
- shadow-dom.md
- tabs.md
- uploads.md
- viewport.md

## What actually works

- Screenshots first: use capture_screenshot() to understand the current page quickly, find visible targets, and decide whether you need a click, a selector, or more navigation.
- Clicking: capture_screenshot() → read the pixel off the image → click_at_xy(x, y) → capture_screenshot() to verify. Suppress the Playwright-habit reflex of "locate first, then click" — no getBoundingClientRect, no selector hunt. Drop to DOM only when the target has no visible geometry (hidden input, 0×0 node). Hit-testing happens in Chrome's browser process, so clicks go through iframes / shadow DOM / cross-origin without extra work.
- Bulk HTTP: http_get(url) + ThreadPoolExecutor. No browser for static pages (249 Netflix pages in 2.8s).
- After goto: wait_for_load().
- Wrong/stale tab: ensure_real_tab(). Use it when the current tab is stale or internal; the daemon also auto-recovers from stale sessions on the next call.
- Verification: print(page_info()) is the simplest "is this alive?" check, but screenshots are the default way to verify whether a visible action actually worked.
- DOM reads: use js(...) for inspection and extraction when the screenshot shows that coordinates are the wrong tool.
- Iframe sites (Azure blades, Salesforce): click_at_xy(x, y) passes through; only drop to iframe DOM work when coordinate clicks are the wrong tool.
- Auth wall: redirected to login → stop and ask the user. Don't type credentials from screenshots.
- Raw CDP for anything helpers don't cover: cdp("Domain.method", params).

## Design constraints

- Coordinate clicks default. Input.dispatchMouseEvent goes through iframes/shadow/cross-origin at the compositor level.
- Connect to the user's running Chrome. Don't launch your own browser.
- cdp-use is only for CDPClient.send_raw. Prefer raw CDP strings over typed wrappers.
- run.py stays tiny. No argparse, subcommands, or extra control layer.
- Core helpers stay short. Put task-specific helper additions in `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`; daemon/bootstrap and remote session admin live in the core package.
- Don't add a manager layer. No retries framework, session manager, daemon supervisor, config system, or logging framework.

## Gotchas (field-tested)

- Omnibox popups are fake page targets. Filter chrome://omnibox-popup... and other internals when you need a real tab.
- CDP target order != Chrome's visible tab-strip order. Use UI automation when the user means "the first/second tab I can see"; Target.activateTarget only shows a known target.
- Default daemon sessions can go stale. ensure_real_tab() re-attaches to a real page.
- Browser Use API is camelCase on the wire. cdpUrl, proxyCountryCode, etc.
- Remote cdpUrl is HTTPS, not ws. Resolve the websocket URL via /json/version.
- Stop cloud browsers with PATCH /browsers/{id} + {"action":"stop"}.
- After every meaningful action, re-screenshot before assuming it worked. Use the image to verify changed state, open menus, navigation, visible errors, and whether the page is in the state you expected.
- Use screenshots to drive exploration. They are often the fastest way to find the next click target, notice hidden blockers, and decide if a selector is even worth writing.
- Prefer compositor-level actions over framework hacks. Try screenshots, coordinate clicks, and raw key input before adding DOM-specific workarounds.
- If you need framework-specific DOM tricks, check interaction-skills/ first. That is where dropdown, dialog, iframe, shadow DOM, and form-specific guidance belongs.

## Domain skills (opt-in)

Only applies when `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1`. Otherwise ignore — `agent-workspace/domain-skills/` is dormant and `goto_url` won't surface skill files.

When enabled, search `agent-workspace/domain-skills/<host>/` before inventing an approach. `goto_url` returns up to 10 skill filenames for the navigated host.

If you learn anything non-obvious — a private API, stable selector, framework quirk, URL pattern, hidden wait, or site-specific trap — open a PR to `agent-workspace/domain-skills/<site>/`. Capture the durable shape of the site (the map, not the diary). Don't write pixel coordinates (break on layout), task narration, or secrets — the directory is public.

# Hermes Agent

Hermes Agent is an open-source AI agent framework by Nous Research that runs in your terminal, messaging platforms, and IDEs. It belongs to the same category as Claude Code (Anthropic), Codex (OpenAI), and OpenClaw — autonomous coding and task-execution agents that use tool calling to interact with your system. Hermes works with any LLM provider (OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek, local models, and 15+ others) and runs on Linux, macOS, and WSL.

What makes Hermes different:

- **Self-improving through skills** — Hermes learns from experience by saving reusable procedures as skills. When it solves a complex problem, discovers a workflow, or gets corrected, it can persist that knowledge as a skill document that loads into future sessions. Skills accumulate over time, making the agent better at your specific tasks and environment.
- **Persistent memory across sessions** — remembers who you are, your preferences, environment details, and lessons learned. Pluggable memory backends (built-in, Honcho, Mem0, and more) let you choose how memory works.
- **Multi-platform gateway** — the same agent runs on Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, Matrix, Email, and 10+ other platforms with full tool access, not just chat.
- **Provider-agnostic** — swap models and providers mid-workflow without changing anything else. Credential pools rotate across multiple API keys automatically.
- **Profiles** — run multiple independent Hermes instances with isolated configs, sessions, skills, and memory.
- **Extensible** — plugins, MCP servers, custom tools, webhook triggers, cron scheduling, and the full Python ecosystem.

People use Hermes for software development, research, system administration, data analysis, content creation, home automation, and anything else that benefits from an AI agent with persistent context and full system access.

**This skill helps you work with Hermes Agent effectively** — setting it up, configuring features, spawning additional agent instances, troubleshooting issues, finding the right commands and settings, and understanding how the system works when you need to extend or contribute to it.

**Docs:** https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/

## Security & Privacy Toggles

Common "why is Hermes doing X to my output / tool calls / commands?" toggles — and the exact commands to change them. Most of these need a fresh session (`/reset` in chat, or start a new `hermes` invocation) because they're read once at startup.

### Secret redaction in tool output

Secret redaction is **off by default** — tool output (terminal stdout, `read_file`, web content, subagent summaries, etc.) passes through unmodified. If the user wants Hermes to auto-mask strings that look like API keys, tokens, and secrets before they enter the conversation context and logs:

```bash
hermes config set security.redact_secrets true       # enable globally
```

**Restart required.** `security.redact_secrets` is snapshotted at import time — toggling it mid-session (e.g. via `export HERMES_REDACT_SECRETS=true` from a tool call) will NOT take effect for the running process. Tell the user to run `hermes config set security.redact_secrets true` in a terminal, then start a new session. This is deliberate — it prevents an LLM from flipping the toggle on itself mid-task.

Disable again with:
```bash
hermes config set security.redact_secrets false
```

### PII redaction in gateway messages

Separate from secret redaction. When enabled, the gateway hashes user IDs and strips phone numbers from the session context before it reaches the model:

```bash
hermes config set privacy.redact_pii true    # enable
hermes config set privacy.redact_pii false   # disable (default)
```

### Command approval prompts

By default (`approvals.mode: manual`), Hermes prompts the user before running shell commands flagged as destructive (`rm -rf`, `git reset --hard`, etc.). The modes are:

- `manual` — always prompt (default)
- `smart` — use an auxiliary LLM to auto-approve low-risk commands, prompt on high-risk
- `off` — skip all approval prompts (equivalent to `--yolo`)

```bash
hermes config set approvals.mode smart       # recommended middle ground
hermes config set approvals.mode off         # bypass everything (not recommended)
```

Per-invocation bypass without changing config:
- `hermes --yolo …`
- `export HERMES_YOLO_MODE=1`

Note: YOLO / `approvals.mode: off` does NOT turn off secret redaction. They are independent.

### Shell hooks allowlist

Some shell-hook integrations require explicit allowlisting before they fire. Managed via `~/.hermes/shell-hooks-allowlist.json` — prompted interactively the first time a hook wants to run.

### Disabling the web/browser/image-gen tools

To keep the model away from network or media tools entirely, open `hermes tools` and toggle per-platform. Takes effect on next session (`/reset`). See the Tools & Skills section above.
